Asra Nomani is senior editor of investigations at Fox News Digital. She is a former reporter at the Wall Street Journal, where she covered stories related to money, politics and society. She is the author of "Woke Army: The Left-Green Alliance That Is Undermining America’s Freedom." She can be reached at asra.nomani@fox.com and on X at @asranomani.

title: El-Sayed mocked for 'word salad' answer when pressed by conservative on voting for him: 'Worse than Kamala's'
summary: Abdul El-Sayed's town hall remarks referring to pregnant women as "adult or juvenile human" drew fierce backlash in the Michigan Senate race.
story: Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed referred to a pregnant woman as "an adult" or "juvenile human" while discussing abortion during a "Students vs. Billionaires" town hall at Western Michigan University on Monday.

Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed sparked mockery online over his "word salad" response in which he referred to a pregnant woman as "an adult" or "juvenile human" after a pro-life student asked why he should vote for a progressive candidate like him.

El-Sayed, a vocal supporter of codifying Roe v. Wade into law and funding Planned Parenthood, was speaking to students and prospective voters during a "Students vs. Billionaires" town hall at Western Michigan University on Monday.

"I respect your position insofar as it's founded in the idea that you want to protect and empower life," El-Sayed said to the student. "The question we have to ask ourselves is, what's the best way to do that? And whose life gets destroyed in that process?

"Because too often when government says that you cannot have reproductive care, you are creating a circumstance in which an adult, or sometimes even a juvenile human, is being reduced into simply a carrying vehicle for a fetus that has not ever breathed air," El-Sayed continued.
MICHIGAN GOP LAWMAKER CASTS DOUBT ON EL-SAYED’S SOCIALIST DENIAL AS POLICIES TELL ANOTHER STORY: ‘SHARP ODDS’

Abdul El-Sayed, US Democratic Senate candidate from Michigan, speaks during the Michigan Democratic Party's 2026 nominating convention in Lansing, Michigan, US, on Saturday, Aug. 29, 2026. (Sarah Rice/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
He went on to further emphasize that "the currently existing life of the mother" turns "that person simply into a carrying vehicle for a fetus" when abortion access is taken away.
Conservative critics on social media also quickly weighed in on El-Sayed’s comments, accusing him of using dehumanizing language.
EL-SAYED TORCHED ONLINE AFTER UNEASY UNION MEMBER STRUGGLES THROUGH CAMPAIGN EVENT
Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate, speaks at the Michigan Democratic Nominating Convention in Lansing, Mich., on Aug. 29, 2026. (Anadolu via Getty Images)
In a post on X, RNC Research, an account managed by the Republican National Committee, wrote, "Abdul El-Sayed won’t even say the word woman while talking about pregnancy."

"Abdul El-Sayed just said abortion restrictions turn an 'adult or juvenile human' into 'simply a carrying vehicle for a fetus that has not ever breathed air in the world,'" Mark Levin Show producer Rich Sementa also posted on X. "He won't even say WOMAN. The baby hasn't 'breathed air' so it's just cargo. This is the Democrat Party in 2026."
"This might be worse than Kamala’s word salad," Great Lakes HQ, an account run by the super PAC Great Lakes Conservatives Fund, posted on X.

"So much euphemism and jargon in here that it's hard to keep track, all in the cause of avoiding saying that women should be able to abort their babies with no restriction," National Review's Rich Lowry posted on X.
"Nobody talks like that in real life," Grabien Media founder Tom Elliott posted on X.
MICHIGAN DEMOCRAT AWKWARDLY PIVOTS TO CIRCUMCISION DURING HEATED FOX NEWS DEBATE ON CHILD SEX CHANGES

Former Rep. Mike Rogers, a Republican from Michigan and US Senate candidate, during the second day of the Republican Midterm Convention at the American Airlines Center in Dallas, Texas, on Thursday, Sept. 10, 2026. (Mark Felix/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
"And we're supposed to believe that this guy is a doctor," Amy Curtis, a writer at Townhall, posted on X.
In a statement to Fox News Digital, former GOP gubernatorial candidate Tudor Dixon accused El-Sayed of trying to change the way people think about motherhood and having children.
"Radicals like Abdul El-Sayed use language that removes the gentle, loving relationship between mothers and their children to achieve their goal of destroying the American family," Dixon said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Ahead of the high-stakes November race that could determine control of the Senate, El-Sayed's positions on abortion, LGBTQ+ rights and gender-affirming care for minors have been thrust into the spotlight. He has also repeatedly rejected the socialist label, describing himself as a capitalist.
El-Sayed will face Republican Senate nominee Mike Rogers for the seat being vacated by retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters.
Fox News Digital reached out to El-Sayed’s campaign for comment.
Kiera McDonald is a Production Assistant for Fox News Digital.

title: Virginia school district faces probe over 9/11 teaching guide telling teachers not to ‘center the extremists’
summary: America First Legal launched a FOIA investigation into Fairfax County Public Schools' 9/11 guidance that tells teachers not to center extremists.
story: America First Legal senior counsel Ian Prior tells Fox News Digital why the group is investigating Fairfax County Public Schools in Virginia after controversial 9/11 teaching guidance was initially reported.

EXCLUSIVE: America First Legal (AFL) has launched an investigation into Fairfax County Public Schools (FCPS) in Virginia after Fox News Digital first exposed controversial guidance for teaching the 9/11 terrorist attacks, seeking to determine who was responsible for developing instructions that tell teachers not to "center the extremists or the acts of the extremists."
The conservative legal group announced the investigation after Fox News Digital first reported on the FCPS guide ahead of the 25th anniversary of the attacks.
The district's guidance tells teachers not to "associate the 9/11 attacks with Islam or Muslims" or "center the extremists or the acts of the extremists."
LIBERAL VIRGINIA SCHOOL DISTRICT: DON'T LINK 9/11 TERROR ATTACKS TO 'ISLAM or MUSLIMS'
AFL is seeking to examine how the school district arrived at the guidance for teaching 9/11 to students. (Salwan Georges/The Washington Post via Getty Images, File)
"We wanna know where this comes from. We wanna know who the school is working with to develop these guidances," America First Legal senior counsel Ian Prior told Fox News Digital.

Prior said AFL is seeking to examine how FCPS arrived at the guidance and whether any outside organizations participated in its development, but acknowledged AFL has not yet determined whether that occurred.
"We're still seeking to determine how far this goes," Prior said. "That's why we're investigating so that we can get to the bottom of it."
The investigation was directly prompted by Fox News Digital's reporting, Prior said.
CBC RELEASES POLICY CHANGE AFTER CONTROVERSY ABOUT REFUSING TO REFER TO 9/11 AS ‘TERRORIST ATTACKS’

Fairfax County Public Schools provides teachers with a guide that includes "critical considerations" to avoid discussing the extremist interpretation of Islam that motivated the 9/11 hijackers. (Fairfax County Public Schools)

"The reason why we're investigating now is because this was just reported," he said, adding that AFL saw the report "just like everybody else" and wanted to determine who FCPS was working with when the guidance was developed.

In announcing its investigation, AFL is accusing the school district of attempting to "sanitize history" and calling for "full transparency regarding who is responsible" for the guidance. The group's announcement directs readers to a Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) request, though the two-page release itself does not detail the records sought.

The six-page FCPS guide, titled "25th Anniversary and Commemoration of 9/11," was published Aug. 27 and edited Aug. 31. It directs teachers who choose to commemorate the attacks to carefully follow the district's guidance and use only instructional resources available through the district's Atlas site.

FCPS tells educators that lessons about the attacks can unintentionally stigmatize Muslim and Middle Eastern students and instructs teachers to prepare for anti-Muslim rhetoric, create "safe spaces" for Muslim and Middle Eastern students and challenge expressions of bias.
A GENERATION CANNOT REMEMBER 9/11. WE HAVE A DUTY TO MAKE SURE THEY LEARN
Fairfax County Public Schools provides teachers a guidance on teaching about the 9/11 attacks with an emphasis on challenging "anti-Muslim racism." (Fairfax County Public Schools)

Fairfax County Public Schools did not directly answer Fox News Digital's questions about who authored and approved the guidance, whether outside organizations were involved in its development or whether the district has made or considered changes to the document. The district referred Fox News Digital to a statement published on Sept. 11.

In that statement, Superintendent Michelle Reid said FCPS "unequivocally condemn[s]" the 9/11 terrorist attacks and emphasized the district's connection to the Pentagon, military families, first responders and survivors.

The statement also said FCPS was "reviewing our materials" in response to community feedback, while maintaining that "the actions of terrorists should not define the entirety of any faith, culture, or community."
FCPS's Sept. 11 statement provides some information about how the materials were reviewed, but does not identify who authored the six-page guide or who approved its final language.
Prior argued that schools can teach students about the ideology that motivated the Sept. 11 terrorists without assigning collective responsibility to Muslims.
BROOKLYN TEACHERS WHO WITNESSED 9/11 AS CHILDREN REVEAL WHAT THEY WANT THE NEXT GENERATION TO REMEMBER
For elementary students, the district suggests teachers could open by saying, "Twenty-five years ago today, there was an attack on the United States." (iStock)
The district's guidance similarly states that teachers should make clear that al Qaeda carried out the attacks, while drawing a distinction between the terrorist organization and Muslims as a whole.

"When discussing this topic with students, please make clear that the September 11 attacks were carried out by Al-Qaeda, a terrorist extremist organization," the guide states. "Al-Qaeda’s ideology and actions should not be attributed to Islam or to Muslims as a religious community."
The dispute centers in part on how much emphasis teachers should place on the terrorists and their ideology when commemorating the attacks.

FCPS tells teachers that "the commemoration of 9/11 focuses on those whose lives were lost and those who sacrificed to help others — not those who attacked the United States." The guide encourages teachers to emphasize stories of "resilience, support, and resistance" and use age-appropriate details about the violence.
CBC CAVES ON 9/11 ‘TERRORISM’ GUIDANCE AS US, CANADIAN OFFICIALS UNLEASH CROSS-BORDER BACKLASH
Flowers and American flags are seen next to inscribed names at a reflecting pool at the National September 11 Memorial & Museum on Sept. 11, in New York City. (Jeenah Moon/Pool/Getty Images)

For elementary students, the district suggests teachers could open by saying, "Twenty-five years ago today, there was an attack on the United States," before allowing students' questions to determine what additional information is shared at the teacher's professional discretion.

Its suggested language for older students is considerably more specific, stating that "members of the extremist group al-Qaeda hijacked four planes in a coordinated terrorist attack on the United States" before recounting the 2,977 people killed, including civilians, military personnel at the Pentagon and emergency workers. The guidance also highlights the passengers and crew of Flight 93 who fought back against the hijackers.

FCPS said in the guide that its approach reflects the varied experiences of families in the Northern Virginia district, where some were personally affected by the attacks and the ensuing War on Terror.

"Many families of military personnel and first responders experienced loss and hardship," the document states, while also saying Muslim families worry about harassment and hate crimes surrounding the anniversary.
AFL argues the district's approach goes too far.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"Fairfax County Public Schools is attempting to sanitize history and erase the radical Islamic terrorism that struck our nation on September 11, 2001," AFL counsel Will Scolinos said in announcing the investigation. "Parents and the public must have full transparency regarding who is responsible for stripping truth from our children’s classrooms."
Prior said AFL has not determined what action could ultimately follow its investigation and that the group's next steps will depend on what it finds.
Fox News Digital's Asra Nomani contributed to this reporting.
Jasmine Baehr is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital, where she covers politics, the military, legal debates surrounding life and family policy, as well as faith and culture.

title: Beyond killer robots: China's real AI threat to America is already here, experts warn
summary: Experts warn Chinese labs are using "knowledge distillation" and free software to undercut U.S. tech dominance, bypass billions in research and supercharge cognitive warfare.
story: Experts Gordon Chang and Leah Siskind detail Beijing's strategy to leapfrog U.S. technology, using knowledge distillation, low-cost open models and embodied AI.

While Americans brace for a futuristic AI war of killer robots and bioweapons, experts warn ahead of President Xi Jinping's U.S. visit this week that Beijing is already actively undermining America's global supremacy through AI without ever firing a shot.

Experts who spoke with Fox News Digital outlined a stealthy, three-part playbook, which includes extracting the logic of American models, undercutting U.S. developers with free open-source software and ultimately weaponizing those systems for things like cognitive warfare.

They laid out how China bypasses billions of dollars in U.S. research through labs that interrogate cutting-edge American AI and copy its capabilities, while simultaneously flooding the global market with free alternatives.

"I think a ‘race’ is the wrong metaphor for this," Leah Siskind, an AI research fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, told Fox News Digital. "I think it's kind of like a multi-front war. And in some places, we're winning, and some places we're losing."
XI PREPARES CHINA ‘FOR BATTLE’ AS EXPERT WARNS OF GRAVE DANGER FACING US AHEAD OF DC SUMMIT
Chinese President Xi Jinping, left, shakes hands with U.S. President Donald Trump at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing May 14, 2026. (Kenny Holston/Pool Photo via AP)

While top American tech firms have poured billions into building ultra-expensive, proprietary systems, China has focused heavily on distributing free, open-source models across the globe. Siskind warned that because American tech is costly and the U.S. sector has largely neglected open-source investment, many Fortune 500 companies are making the financial choice to run their operations on Chinese models, unwittingly opening the door to potential CCP censorship, hidden backdoors and, ultimately, global dominance.

"How can you compete with something that's free when American tech is very, very expensive?" Siskind said. "How can we ensure that a Chinese open-source model would be truly clean, that it'd be truly free of CCP censorship? We can't be — we just wouldn't know. And that's by design. We wouldn't know what sort of trick backdoors might be implanted and how that could rear its head later on."
China expert Gordon Chang warned that Beijing is intentionally using these free models to repeat an economic tactic it previously deployed to corner a different industry.

"This is a tactic that China used with solar panels," Chang told Fox News Digital. "Beijing sees that one day it will drive out the American models on cost and availability, and they will then dominate global AI."

CHAD WOLF: CONGRESS HAS A CHANCE TO STOP CHINA FROM TURNING YOUR CAR INTO A CHINESE SPYBut to flood the market with free software, Beijing first needs the underlying technology and a way to bypass America's massive lead in computing power.
Gordon Chang, a prominent China expert, said the United States does "not want our elections determined in China." (Fox News Digital)

Chang noted that the U.S. possesses a commanding lead in physical infrastructure, boasting over 5,400 data centers compared to China's roughly 450, along with far superior microchips. To work around the staggering hardware and energy costs required to train artificial intelligence from scratch, Siskind warned that Chinese labs are closing the gap through a process known as "knowledge distillation," a method where a smaller model essentially interrogates a larger, smarter American model to copy its logic.

"They are able to leapfrog the process by kind of stealing this information," Siskind said, pointing to the Chinese model DeepSeek as a prime example. "This is how they were able to release models like DeepSeek in 2025, which was seismic news because they were able to show that they were really competing with cutting-edge American models and had invested a fraction of the resources."
US ADVERSARY TURNS UP THE HEAT ON AMERICA’S AI LEAD WITH AN UNDERESTIMATED EDGE

The threat is not theoretical. Just last week, the Department of Homeland Security issued a joint cybersecurity advisory warning that Chinese companies are conducting "industrial-scale knowledge distillation campaigns" to extract proprietary capabilities from U.S. frontier models.
Leah Siskind, an AI research fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, says China is waging a "multi-front war" with AI. (Fox News)
Beyond economic undercutting and software theft, the experts also warned Beijing is simultaneously deploying artificial intelligence into physical supply chains and public influence campaigns.

Rather than sci-fi "killer robots," Siskind emphasized that China's immediate physical priority is "embodied AI," embedding artificial intelligence into real-world infrastructure like factory automation, commercial drones and autonomous supply chains.
Chang warned that AI-enhanced propaganda poses a direct threat to American decision-making and democratic sovereignty.

"They're very good at cognitive warfare, and they can enhance their capabilities with artificial intelligence," Chang said. "We do not want our elections determined in China. We do not want our critical national security decisions being made in Beijing. And that's not impossible."
CHINA EXPERT WARNS BEIJING WANTS AMERICANS — NOT THE CCP — TO SPREAD ITS MESSAGE

As President Xi Jinping arrives in the U.S. this week, the experts who spoke to Fox News Digital said the White House must treat these non-cinematic threats with the same urgency as traditional military posturing.
Chinese President Xi Jinping March 23, 2019, in Rome, Italy. (Antonio Masiello/Getty Images)

To protect America's remaining edge, Siskind said Washington must tighten chip export loopholes, blacklist foreign labs engaging in deceptive distillation and incentivize U.S. open-source development, emphasizing that "it is very important that the most advanced systems are developed under democracy and represent democratic values, as opposed to authoritarian values."
CHINA-LINKED HACKERS INFILTRATED US GOVERNMENT NETWORKS BEFORE FBI TAKEDOWN
For Chang, the stakes of that technological defense extend far beyond standard economic competition.

"Xi Jinping throughout this century has been pushing the Chinese imperial-era notion of Tianxia, or 'all under heaven' that China's rulers have a right to rule the world," Chang warned. "That sounds ludicrous to us, but a Chinese regime powered by AI might actually be able to accomplish that. We certainly do not want our decisions being made in the Chinese capital."
China is accused of stealing U.S. AI technology.  (Kritsapong Jieantaratip via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Addressing the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday, President Donald Trump reiterated Washington's goal of outpacing China, declaring that U.S. government documents will now refer to AI as "superintelligence."

"The United States totally rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme to control the artificial intelligence being spoken of," Trump told world leaders. "Whoever wins superintelligence wins. And we're leading now over China by a lot and everyone else. And we're going to keep it that way."
Alec Schemmel is a Politics Reporter for Fox News Digital who is originally from Charlotte, North Carolina but now resides in the Washington D.C.-Baltimore Metro Area.

title: Former USPS worker indicted after allegedly dumping 300-plus Utah mail-in ballots without delivering one
summary: Damon Matai Seei allegedly separated over 300 mail-in ballots from other mail at the start of his shift and discarded them within 90 minutes.
story: The Department of Justice announces Tuesday the indictment of former Utah letter carrier Damon Matai Seei, for allegedly destroying over 300 mail-in ballots. The DOJ emphasizes ongoing efforts under President Donald Trump to secure elections.

A former U.S. Postal Service (USPS) worker in Utah was indicted after allegedly setting aside more than 300 mail-in ballots at the start of his shift and dumping them without delivering a single one, Department of Justice (DOJ) officials said on charges related to the case Tuesday.

Damon Matai Seei, 34, of Payson, Utah, was indicted by a federal grand jury on Sept. 16, on a charge related to the unlawful secretion, destruction and delay of mail. He was arrested Tuesday and made his initial appearance in federal court in Salt Lake City.

Federal prosecutors allege Seei was working as a letter carrier on June 3, when he was entrusted with delivering mail to more than 300 people in Eagle Mountain, Utah, ahead of the state's June 23 primary election.
USPS WOULDN'T DELIVER BALLOTS IN STATES THAT REFUSE TO FORK OVER MAIL-IN VOTER INFO UNDER PROPOSED RULE
A mail-in ballot sent to voters in Eagle Mountain, Utah, ahead of the June 23, 2026, primary election. (Department of Justice)
The mail included advertisements and hundreds of mail-in ballots that were clearly marked as ballots, according to DOJ officials.

Officials said Seei separated the ballots from other mail shortly after beginning his shift, did not deliver any of them and discarded them roughly 90 minutes later. Other mail was also discarded, officials said.
Several voters later complained to the Utah County Clerk that they had not received their mail-in ballots, U.S. Attorney Melissa Holyoak for the District of Utah said Tuesday.
POSTAL SERVICE THRUST INTO MAIL-IN BALLOT FIGHT AS TRUMP ORDER GETS TIED UP IN COURT
A dumpster in a church parking lot where prosecutors allege a former postal worker discarded mail, including hundreds of mail-in ballots. (Department of Justice)
Using county databases, the clerk determined that voter participation was unusually low in the area where the complaints originated, according to Holyoak.

It remains unclear whether the affected voters ultimately received replacement ballots or were able to vote. Holyoak said federal officials are continuing to investigate and plan to contact affected voters to determine whether they were able to cast ballots.
Seei has told investigators that he did not have a political motive, according to DOJ officials. The investigation remains ongoing.
SEVEN NONCITIZENS CHARGED IN NORTH TEXAS ELECTION-INTEGRITY INVESTIGATION
A person holding their ballot before placing it in a mailbox during U.S. elections. (iStock)

"When American voters lawfully cast their vote, they should feel confident that it is counted," said Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter. "Allegedly throwing away hundreds of ballots is a serious federal crime that undermines the integrity of our elections. Ballot integrity is not a partisan issue."

The case was investigated jointly by the USPS of Inspector General and Homeland Security Investigations (HSI).
Seei's next court appearance is scheduled for Nov. 30.
Brittany Miller is a Fox News Digital breaking news writer and former Independent reporter who graduated from Syracuse University in 2023.

title: Fox News Poll: Voters question whether AI’s promise outweighs its risks
summary: A Fox News survey finds 71% oppose AI data centers in their area, but 52% favor remote locations, revealing a stark NIMBY divide among voters.
story: Former CIA station Chief Dan Hoffman unpacks concerns over malicious activity in AI and remembers the victims of the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks on 'America Reports.'

As artificial intelligence becomes increasingly politicized ahead of the midterm elections, the latest Fox News national survey finds voters struggling to reconcile the technology’s promise with the economic and environmental costs of the data centers needed to power it.
They are especially against allowing centers in their communities while favoring them in remote locations, creating a "Not In My Backyard" dynamic.

A 71% majority opposes building AI data centers in their area, including 46% who strongly oppose them. Both of those numbers are up a touch since earlier this summer. However, the survey reveals a paradox: a 52% majority favors building them in remote locations (44% oppose).
FOX NEWS POLL: SQUEEZED BY COSTS, FRUSTRATED VOTERS TURN TO THE DEMOCRATS

The central contrast is seen across community types, as about 7 in 10 urban, suburban and rural voters oppose data centers in their backyards. That consensus fades regarding remote facilities. Half of urban voters (50%) and a majority of suburban voters (57%) favor building them there, while 51% of rural voters remain opposed.

Women, White voters, those without a college degree and Democrats are more likely than men, non-White voters, college graduates and Republicans to oppose data centers, whether near their community or elsewhere.

When presented with arguments for and against data centers, reactions are nuanced. By roughly 30 points, voters are less likely to support construction if told data centers could strain local water supplies (by 28 points), raise energy bills (29 points) or grow to an enormous size (29 points).
FOX NEWS POLL: 71% THINK TRUMP ADMINISTRATION LACKS PLAN TO END IRAN WAR

Opposition softens when voters see direct benefits to daily life or national interests. They are more likely to be supportive if told data centers are necessary for online activities such as streaming and banking (9 points), critical infrastructure like transportation and water systems (13 points) or to help maintain a competitive edge over countries like China (18 points).

These reactions to additional information operate against a backdrop of AI pessimism. Majorities of voters are more likely to see AI as bad rather than good for the U.S. economy (54% bad vs. 36% good), mental health (54-34%), society (56-34%), the environment (60-30%) and jobs (63-29%).
The lone exception is day-to-day life, where more voters say AI is a good thing by 4 points (47% good, 43% bad), down from an 11-point spread in November 2025 (50-39%).

Overall, AI technology is viewed more negatively than positively by 23 points (37% favorable vs. 60% unfavorable), widening from an 11-point deficit in April and 9 points in July. The underlying demographic patterns mirror those for data centers. Democrats (67% unfavorable), White voters without a college degree (65%), women (64%) and independents (64%) are the most negative. The most favorable views come from non-White men (49% favorable), voters with graduate degrees (49%) and MAGA Republicans (46%).
AI & The 2026 Midterms

On the generic congressional ballot, the Democratic candidate is ahead of the Republican by 7 points overall. Republicans have a 21-point advantage among voters who support building data centers in their communities, narrowing to 9 points among those allowing construction only in remote areas. Democrats are ahead by at least 19 points among voters who oppose data centers in either location.
Voters who view AI favorably back the Republican candidate in their district by 7 points, while those with unfavorable views back the Democrat by 17 points.

"In this election, the bottom line is that technology is no longer just a tool. It’s a wedge issue," said Republican pollster Daron Shaw, who conducts the Fox News Poll with Democrat Chris Anderson. "As infrastructure demands force AI into the physical world, campaigns that map tech anxiety onto their voter coalitions will shape the midterm narrative."

Voters think Democrats would better handle building AI data centers by a 14-point margin. That lead is especially strong among Black voters (D +51), voters under age 30 (D +35), Hispanic voters (D +29), and independents (D +26). It narrows among White voters (D +5) and rural voters (D +7), while White rural voters are one of the few groups to say Republicans would do better (R +4). Cross-party defections also advantage the Democrats: 15% of Republicans prefer Democrats on data centers, compared with just 4% of Democrats favoring Republicans.
A few more things…
Three-quarters of voters (76%) favor banning AI in kindergarten through eighth grade classrooms, with some of the strongest preference for the ban among moms (81%).
CLICK HERE FOR CROSSTABS AND TOPLINE
Support for banning cellphones in K-12 classrooms is also high: 72% favor the policy and 25% oppose it.
In addition, a majority supports prohibiting police departments from using automated license plate readers, such as Flock Safety cameras (57% favor vs. 39% oppose).

Age creates the biggest divide. Voters under 30 would ban license plate readers by 28 points, while those 65 and over support them by 7 points. Partisans show unusual agreement on banning the cameras, though by different margins: Democrats by 27 points, independents by 23 points and Republicans by 6 points.

Conducted September 11-14, 2026, under the direction of Beacon Research (D) and Shaw & Company Research (R), this Fox News survey includes interviews with a sample of 1,211 registered voters randomly selected from a national voter file. Respondents spoke with live interviewers on landlines (96) and cellphones (821) or completed the survey online after receiving a text (294). Results based on the full sample have a margin of sampling error of ±3 percentage points. Sampling error for results among subgroups is higher. In addition to sampling error, question wording and order can influence results. Weights are generally applied to age, race, education and area variables to ensure the demographics are representative of the registered voter population. Sources for developing weight targets include the most recent American Community Survey, Fox News Voter Analysis and voter file data.

title: Biden administration granted woman green card months before she illegally voted in 2024 election: DHS
summary: Evelyn Miller of the Philippines registered online weeks before Election Day and voted in the 2024 election in Pennsylvania despite not being a U.S. citizen, DOJ says.
story: Fox News correspondent Brooke Taylor gets an exclusive ride-along with Homeland Security agents as they ramp up arrests of immigrants accused of participating in voter fraud. The report provides a behind-the-scenes look at the agency's enforcement efforts, the investigative process targeting alleged election-related offenses and the broader push to safeguard election integrity on 'The Story.'
A Biden-era noncitizen from the Philippines living in Pennsylvania pleaded guilty to illegally voting in the 2024 election after registering just weeks before Election Day, federal prosecutors said.
Evelyn Miller, 37, of Emmaus, pleaded guilty Sept. 16, to illegally voting in the election.
Miller is a lawful permanent resident but not a U.S. citizen, the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania said.
Only U.S. citizens can vote in federal elections.
ICE ARRESTS PERUVIAN NATIONAL ACCUSED OF ILLEGALLY VOTING IN 2024 ELECTION AS DHS CITES SIMILAR CASES
Evelyn Miller, 37, of Emmaus, Pa., pleaded guilty to illegally voting in the 2024 general election. (Department of Homeland Security)

Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) began looking into Miller after receiving information that someone living in Lehigh County may have illegally registered to vote or cast a ballot, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said Tuesday.
DHS said Miller registered online on Oct. 9, 2024, less than a month before she voted in person in the Nov. 5 general election.

HSI and FBI agents interviewed Miller at her home in July 2025. Miller told investigators she registered online before the election and then went to her polling place in Emmaus to vote on Election Day, according to DHS.
SEVEN NONCITIZENS CHARGED IN NORTH TEXAS ELECTION-INTEGRITY INVESTIGATION
Mullin said the federal election cycle was central to the country and argued that citizenship verification should not be controversial. (Leigh Green for Fox News Digital)
Miller had received lawful permanent resident status July 19, 2024, during the Biden administration, DHS said.
"This alien from the Philippines pleaded guilty to illegally voting in the 2024 election in Pennsylvania," DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said.

"Thanks to the hard work of the men and women of HSI, as well as our partners at the Department of Justice, this alien will soon face justice for her efforts to subvert our elections. American elections are for Americans only."
HSI investigated the case with the FBI.
ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT ARRESTED IN INDIANA FOR ALLEGEDLY VOTING IN FEDERAL ELECTION: DHS

Homeland Security Investigations began looking into Miller after receiving information that someone living in Lehigh County may have illegally registered to vote or cast a ballot. (Jeff Swensen/Getty Images, File)
Miller's case comes as the Justice Department pursues a broader group of election-related cases stemming from the 2024 election.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Federal prosecutors announced Sept. 18 that 16 people had been charged in separate cases involving illegal voting and related election crimes across several states.
Miller is scheduled to be sentenced Dec. 16. She faces up to one year in prison, one year of supervised release and a $100,000 fine, according to federal prosecutors.
Brittany Miller is a Fox News Digital breaking news writer and former Independent reporter who graduated from Syracuse University in 2023.

title: San Francisco sues Trump Media over alleged 'pay-to-play' Truth Social service
summary: San Francisco City Attorney David Chiu alleges the paid service gives wealthy subscribers an unfair advantage by providing early access to President Donald Trump's market-moving posts.
story: San Francisco City Attorney David Chiu announced a lawsuit against Trump Media, alleging the company's paid Truth Social service violates ethics and insider trading laws. (Credit: David Chiu via Facebook)

President Donald Trump's social media company is facing a lawsuit from the city of San Francisco over a paid Truth Social subscription service that gives certain customers early access to the president's posts.

San Francisco City Attorney David Chiu announced the lawsuit Tuesday, alleging that Trump Media's Truth API service operates as a "pay-to-play scheme," allowing subscribers to receive President Donald Trump's market-moving posts before they are publicly available.
The lawsuit seeks to block the service and impose civil penalties under California's Unfair Competition Law (UCL).
Chiu alleged the service gives wealthy subscribers an "unfair advantage" by providing early access to government information before it reaches the broader public.
TRUMP WARNS HE'LL BE 'LAST REPUBLICAN PRESIDENT' IF SENATE GOP DOESN'T MAKE MAJOR CHANGE

President Donald Trump's social media company is facing a lawsuit from the city of San Francisco over a paid Truth Social subscription service that gives certain customers early access to the president's posts. (Anadolu via Getty Images)

"Truth Social has knowingly created a marketplace for insider trading by giving high-paying subscribers an unfair advantage over ordinary investors in the market," Chiu said at a news conference Tuesday. "It's a pay-to-play scheme for early access to the president's market-moving government decisions."

The monthly subscription was rolled out Aug. 1 and costs between $60,000 to $100,000 in exchange for early access to market-moving posts from Truth Social accounts with large followings, including Trump’s own account.

"No ordinary person can pay that fee," Chiu said. "Now the early subscribers are largely high-frequency trading firms with the technology to analyze that information and to make trades within microseconds."
TRUMP ANNOUNCES WHITE HOUSE BAN AGAINST THREE MEDIA OUTLETS
The monthly subscription was rolled out Aug. 1 and costs between $60,000 to $100,000. (Anna Barclay/Getty Images)
Chiu also said Trump owns roughly 41% of Trump Media and "is personally benefiting from this business scheme."

A Trump Media spokesperson pushed back on the allegations, telling Fox News Digital, "The people of California should outsource their future lawsuits to AI chatbots who, unlike the left-wing activists masquerading as attorneys who filed this lawsuit, will grasp the basic distinction between public and nonpublic information."
The lawsuit was filed Monday, the same day that dozens of former federal prosecutors and agents filed a court brief backing a separate lawsuit over Truth API, according to CBS News.
TRUMP’S $100K WALL STREET TRUTH ACCESS DRAWS LAWSUIT; EXPERT WARNS IT ‘RAISES THE STAKES’ ON ETHICS

Chiu alleged the service gives wealthy subscribers an "unfair advantage" by providing early access to government information before it reaches the broader public. (Steve Jennings/Getty Images for TechCrunch)
The separate lawsuit, brought by The Intercept and the Freedom of the Press Foundation, alleges the paid service violates the First and Fifth amendments.

A White House spokesperson referred Fox News Digital to Trump Media and The Trump Organization for comment.
Representatives for The Trump Organization and Chiu's office could not immediately be reached by Fox News Digital for comment.
Fox News Digital's Julia Bonavita contributed to this report.

title: AI robot may stop your dog from barking while you're gone
summary: WIM-Z's AI dog training robot uses on-device processing to detect barking and dispense treats autonomously, with field trials showing up to 83% reduction.
story: Wonderdog chief medical officer Dr. Evan Antin joins 'Fox & Friends' to explain their new AI health companion for dogs. The platform tracks over 40 different analytes from regular at-home blood draws, detecting illnesses like kidney degradation before symptoms manifest. This proactive approach aims to prolong pets' lives and help owners understand their dog's long-term health.

If your dog starts barking the second you walk out the door, leaving home can come with a little extra guilt. That can happen whether you live in an apartment or a house. A pet camera can show you what is happening, but watching from your phone does little when your dog reacts to every sound outside or gets anxious when you are gone.

WIM-Z wants to take a more active role. The small tracked robot uses on-device artificial intelligence to watch your dog and respond to certain behaviors. Once the robot is in position, it can identify your dog, detect barking and decide when to reward calmer behavior with a treat. You can also speak through the robot and drive it around your home from your phone.
AI ROBOT FOR SENIORS CAN ALERT FAMILY AFTER A CALL FOR HELP
WIM-Z is designed to move around the home with your dog, using AI to detect barking and reward calmer behavior with treats. (WIM-Z)
Now WIM-Z has shared early field results, and its first customer units will make behavior and training decisions on their own while owners control where the robot moves.

How the WIM-Z AI dog training robot works

WIM-Z stands for Watchful Intelligent Mobile Zen. The robot measures about 11 inches tall and rides on rubber tank-style treads. Its camera turret can pan 270 degrees and tilt more than 120 degrees. A side cartridge holds up to 44 treats.
Inside, WIM-Z uses a Raspberry Pi 5 with a Hailo-8 AI accelerator. The company says its onboard AI can identify individual dogs, classify barking and track a dog with its pan-and-tilt camera.
Once WIM-Z detects barking, its behavior system can decide whether to intervene without waiting for you. The robot can then use a calming cue and dispense a treat when appropriate.

However, there is an important limit. WIM-Z does not currently drive itself around your home looking for your dog. You control that movement through the app, or you can leave the robot in one location.
WIM-Z also includes two-way audio. Its app can show behavior activity and optional highlight clips, giving you another way to see what happened while you were away.
WIM-Z says barking dropped by as much as 83%

WIM-Z recently released results from seven field trials conducted between May and September 2026. Six took place in homes around the New York metro area. One took place at a kennel in Jersey City. Across the trials, four hand-built robots logged 50 sessions and about 60 hours of use. WIM-Z says the system detected more than 2,100 barks. It also made 107 autonomous interventions and dispensed about 500 rewards.

The biggest numbers came from two homes that ran repeat autonomous sessions over two to three weeks. In one home, barking fell from 161 barks per hour to 40, a 75% reduction. In the other, barking fell from 317 barks per hour to 53, an 83% reduction. WIM-Z also reported that more interventions ended with the dogs going quiet as the trials progressed.
ROBOT DOG COULD DELIVER YOUR NEXT PACKAGE AND AN AD
The WIM-Z robot combines a movable camera, two-way audio and a built-in treat dispenser in its tracked design. (WIM-Z)
Why the reward-based approach stands out

WIM-Z takes a gentler approach. Instead of using shocks, sprays or scolding, it relies on treats and calm cues to reinforce better behavior. That lines up with guidance from the American Veterinary Society of Animal Behavior, which recommends reward-based training and warns against aversive methods.

The bigger question is whether the AI can read the situation well enough to respond appropriately. A dog barking at a delivery person is very different from one that is distressed because you left. WIM-Z has to recognize that difference and react at the right moment for the approach to work well.
What WIM-Z can and cannot do on its own

WIM-Z can handle the behavior side on its own. Its onboard AI can identify a dog, track it with the pan-and-tilt camera, detect barking, decide when to intervene and dispense a reward without you making each decision. What it cannot do yet is navigate your home on its own. You drive WIM-Z from room to room through the app, or you can leave it in one spot where your dog spends time.

The first customer units will work this way, combining autonomous behavior and training features with owner-controlled movement. Full self-navigation, where the robot maps your home and goes looking for your dog by itself, remains on the company's roadmap and will not be included in the first units. So, WIM-Z can decide how to respond to your dog, but you still decide where the robot goes.
What happens to your video and data?

Any mobile robot with a camera and microphone deserves a privacy check before you let it roam around your living room. We asked WIM-Z exactly what happens to the information it collects. The company says all AI processing happens on the robot itself. That includes behavior detection, bark classification and decisions about when to intervene. No video is sent to the cloud for AI analysis.

Some information can still leave the robot. Event data such as bark activity, behavior interventions, treat dispensing and battery status are stored on an Amazon Web Services relay server so it can appear in the app's activity history. If you connect remotely, live video and two-way audio stream through WIM-Z's relay using encrypted WebRTC technology. The company says these are live streams to your phone, not recordings, and they are not stored on its servers.

Optional highlight clips work differently. Short selected clips can be uploaded for assembly and playback in the app, but WIM-Z says continuous footage is never uploaded. Owners can delete clips at any time or turn the feature off completely. The company says those clips are deleted within 90 days after an account is deleted.

WIM-Z also told CyberGuy that it does not sell customer data. Customer footage is not used to train its AI models unless the owner explicitly opts in. When the robot is used only on local Wi-Fi without remote access, the company says nothing leaves the home.

We have raised similar questions with other connected home robots because a camera that can move around your house gets access to very private spaces. Those answers give us a much clearer idea of how WIM-Z handles your information. Still, I would review the privacy controls before bringing any connected camera into my home.
ONE-WHEELED AI SECURITY ROBOT COULD PATROL YOUR PROPERTY
WIM-Z uses its camera and on-device AI to monitor a dog’s behavior and respond with calming cues and rewards. (WIM-Z)
How much WIM-Z costs and when you can get one

WIM-Z will cost $799 for the first production units. Right now, the company is taking a fully refundable $99 deposit to hold a spot. WIM-Z told CyberGuy it expects the first batch to ship from late Q4 2026 through Q1 2027. That means the first units could arrive between the end of 2026 and early 2027.

The company also acknowledges that hardware schedules can slip. If WIM-Z has not shipped your unit by Q2 2027, it says your deposit will be refunded automatically. WIM-Z says the deposits are held through Stripe and are not placed in the company's operating account.

The company says it has built five robots so far. Four are still being used in the field, while another is in Shenzhen, China, for production evaluation with a manufacturer. That gives you a pretty good sense of where things stand. WIM-Z is still in the early stages, so reserving one now means you are getting in before the product has been widely released and used in homes.
What this means to you

If your dog tends to bark or get restless when you leave, WIM-Z shows where pet tech may be headed next. Instead of simply alerting you that something is happening, the robot can respond while you are away by using a calming cue and rewarding your dog when it settles down.

There is one thing to remember with the first version. WIM-Z will not roam around your house looking for your dog by itself. You will need to position it where your dog spends time or drive it remotely through the app.

Still, I would not count on a robot to solve serious separation anxiety. The ASPCA says dogs with moderate or severe separation anxiety may need gradual behavior work with an experienced professional. For barking or mild restlessness, though, a robot that recognizes what your dog is doing and responds at the right time could be a useful extra set of eyes at home.

The early results are interesting, but I want to see what happens when WIM-Z is tested with many more dogs in different homes. I also want to see how well the first production units perform once customers start using them. For now, WIM-Z has an interesting idea, some encouraging early numbers and a much clearer picture of what buyers will actually get.
Kurt's key takeaways

WIM-Z caught my attention because it tackles a problem pet cameras mostly leave in your hands. Seeing your dog bark from miles away can make you feel helpless. WIM-Z's onboard AI can make a training decision and reward calm behavior without waiting for you to step in. I also like that the first version keeps movement in your hands. You control where the robot goes, while the behavior and training system can operate on its own. Full self-navigation may come later. Keeping the AI processing on the robot means your video does not need to go to the cloud for behavior analysis. Remote features and optional highlight clips can still send some information outside your home, so you will want to understand those settings. At $799, I would still want to see more testing and hear from real customers once the first production units start shipping. But if WIM-Z can build on these early results, it could become a useful tool for dog owners who worry about what happens after they walk out the door.

title: AI malware can rewrite itself to evade detection
summary: Google's Threat Intelligence Group found PROMPTFLUX malware that uses Gemini to rewrite its own code every hour, raising urgent cybersecurity alarms.
story: 'The Five' co-hosts discuss AI safety warnings from former President Barack Obama, and governors Gavin Newsom and Kathy Hochul.

Google's Threat Intelligence Group found experimental malware called PROMPTFLUX that could ask Gemini to rewrite its own code. One version was designed to do that every hour. Why would malware keep rewriting itself? To make it harder to recognize.

Security software can look for known patterns in malicious code. If that code keeps changing, the malware becomes a moving target. That does not automatically make it invisible to current security tools, but it can make some types of detection more difficult.

There is an important reality check here. PROMPTFLUX was still being developed when Google found it. Researchers had yet to see it successfully compromise a victim's device or network, and Google disabled assets connected to the activity.

What caught my attention is what came next. Google has since documented AI being used by malware during live attacks. It has also uncovered an Android backdoor that can use AI to understand what is happening on a phone and help decide what to do next. That tells us where this could be heading. So let’s break down how AI-powered malware works and what you can do to protect yourself.
AN AI CYBERATTACK COULD TURN OFF AMERICA'S LIGHTS BEFORE WASHINGTON EVEN UNDERSTANDS WHY
AI-powered malware such as PROMPTFLUX shows how attackers could use AI to keep changing malicious code and make detection harder. (Silas Stein/picture alliance via Getty Images)

Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will show you five practical ways AI can help you organize your health history, remember important appointment details, understand complicated medical information, research prescriptions and prepare smarter questions for your doctor. No technical experience is needed.

How PROMPTFLUX used AI to rewrite itself

PROMPTFLUX was a VBScript-based malware project that Google discovered in June 2025. Its most interesting component was called the "Thinking Robot." The malware could contact Gemini and request new obfuscation techniques designed to make its code harder for security software to recognize.

Google later found multiple PROMPTFLUX variations. One included instructions telling Gemini to rewrite the malware’s entire source code every hour while preserving the pieces needed for it to continue working. Think about what that means from the defender’s side. Security software may identify one version of malicious code. Then the program can generate a different-looking version while continuing to pursue the same goal. That creates a moving target.

Google described PROMPTFLUX as an early example of "just-in-time" AI being built directly into malware. Instead of relying entirely on functions written ahead of time, malware can ask an AI model for help while it runs.
Does rewriting malware make antivirus useless?

No, and this is where I want to be careful. You may hear AI malware described as something that can simply change its appearance and walk right past antivirus protection. The reality has more layers. Signature detection still plays a role in cybersecurity. Security software can recognize the digital fingerprints of known malware and block them quickly.

However, antivirus protection does much more than compare a file with a list of known threats. Microsoft Defender Antivirus, for example, uses real-time monitoring, behavioral analysis and heuristic protection. It also uses cloud-delivered protection and machine learning to help identify new threats that may not match a known malware signature.

That means changing the code does not automatically make malware invisible. A security tool may still notice suspicious behavior once the malware starts doing something dangerous. PROMPTFLUX is concerning because it can make one form of detection harder. That does not mean every layer of modern antivirus suddenly stops working.
PROMPTSTEAL brought AI-powered malware into live attacks

PROMPTFLUX was experimental. PROMPTSTEAL crossed an important line. Google identified the Russian government-backed group APT28 using PROMPTSTEAL against targets in Ukraine. Google says this was its first observation of malware querying a large language model while deployed in live operations.

PROMPTSTEAL takes a different approach from PROMPTFLUX. Instead of asking AI to rewrite itself, it queries the Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct model through Hugging Face. The model generates Windows commands that PROMPTSTEAL can execute.

Those commands can gather information about a computer and copy documents from folders including Documents, Downloads and Desktop. The malware then sends collected information back to infrastructure controlled by the attacker. That is a significant change. The AI model becomes part of what the malware does after it starts running.
PROMPTSPY shows how AI malware could react to your phone

Then came PROMPTSPY. Google detailed the Android backdoor in May 2026 after it was initially identified by ESET. PROMPTSPY contains an AI-powered module called GeminiAutomationAgent. It can send information about what appears on an infected Android device to Gemini and use the response to help navigate the phone’s interface.

In other words, the malware can use AI to understand part of what is happening on the screen and determine how to interact with it. Google found that PROMPTSPY could also make itself harder to remove. When a victim tried to uninstall it, the malware could place an invisible overlay over the uninstall button so taps would appear to do nothing. There is some good news for Android users.

Google says it took action against the actor behind the malware. It also said no apps containing PROMPTSPY were found on Google Play at the time of its May report. Known versions are detected by Google Play Protect, which is enabled by default on Android devices with Google Play Services. Still, PROMPTSPY gives us a much clearer picture of where this technology could go. Malware can begin reacting to the device it finds instead of relying only on instructions written before the attack starts.
HALLUSQUATTING AI ATTACK COULD HIJACK YOUR COMPUTER
Security tools can look beyond known malware signatures by watching for suspicious behavior as malicious code changes. (Uli Deck/picture alliance via Getty Images)
Google’s latest report shows attackers want more automation

Google’s newest report makes the larger trend harder to ignore. On Sept. 8, 2026, Google Threat Intelligence Group said it had seen attackers move from basic AI prompting toward agentic AI workflows and AI-enabled automation. That means AI can start taking on larger pieces of an operation with less human involvement.

One example really jumped out at me. Google says a suspected financially motivated attacker compromised a company’s cloud infrastructure. The attacker then used an AI coding chatbot and agent instructions to plan, build and execute a mass credential-harvesting campaign in less than six hours. The system could manage vulnerability scanning and troubleshoot problems while the attack was underway. Google says thousands of third-party credentials were compromised.

Google has also seen attackers experimenting with automated reconnaissance and frameworks designed to manage harvested credentials. However, there is another important reality check. Google says it has yet to observe threat actors deploying fully autonomous exploit pipelines against targets in the wild. We have not reached the point where an AI system independently launches every part of a cyberattack without people involved. The amount of work AI can take off an attacker’s hands keeps growing, though.
Security teams already face an enormous amount of malware

AI arrives on top of an already huge malware problem. Independent security institute AV-TEST says it registers more than 450,000 new malicious programs and potentially unwanted applications every day. That number does not mean 450,000 completely different attacks are hitting people every day. Malware samples can include different versions and variations of existing threats.

Still, the volume shows why security companies cannot depend on recognizing every malicious file by its appearance alone. Meanwhile, the financial damage tied to cyber-enabled crime continues to climb. The FBI says Americans reported nearly $21 billion in cyber-enabled crime losses during 2025, up 26% from the year before. Those losses cover many kinds of online crime and cannot be attributed to AI malware. However, they show what criminals already stand to gain when technology makes attacks easier to run.
9 ways to protect yourself as malware gets smarter

You do not need to understand how an AI model rewrites VBScript to protect yourself. The best defense still comes from making it harder for malware to reach your device and harder for it to succeed if something slips through.

Look for strong antivirus software with real-time protection and behavioral detection. That becomes especially useful when malicious software changes enough that a traditional signature may not recognize it immediately. The right protection can watch what a program does after it starts running. Suspicious file changes or attempts to alter sensitive system settings can trigger another layer of detection. If you are comparing protection, see our guide to what to look for in antivirus software without the jargon. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.

Security software cannot help as much if its strongest protections have been disabled. On Windows, Microsoft says Defender’s behavior monitoring is enabled by default. Cloud-delivered protection also helps detect new and emerging threats. If a website, pop-up or random tutorial tells you to disable antivirus protection so something will install, stop. Do not turn off security protections to make a questionable download work.

Keep your operating system and browser current. Do the same for software you use regularly. Attackers often look for people running software with vulnerabilities that already have patches available. Automatic updates can close those openings without forcing you to track every security bulletin yourself.
CHINA-LINKED HACKERS INFILTRATED US GOVERNMENT NETWORKS BEFORE FBI TAKEDOWN
Google’s PROMPTSPY research shows how AI could help Android malware interpret what is happening on a phone and decide what to do next. (Philip Dulian/picture alliance via Getty Images)

This has become one of the most important malware warnings I can give you. Attackers increasingly use fake CAPTCHA pages and bogus error messages to tell victims to open Windows Run, PowerShell, Command Prompt or Terminal. The page then asks them to paste a command. Do not do it. A legitimate CAPTCHA should never require you to run a command on your computer. We recently reported that more than 5,400 compromised websites were being used in one campaign built around this trick. See how thousands of hacked sites can trick you into installing malware.

Security warnings can feel annoying when you are trying to download something quickly. Do not automatically click past them. Microsoft Defender SmartScreen, for example, can check websites and downloads for signs of phishing or malicious software. If your browser blocks a file or tells you a site looks dangerous, investigate before continuing. A website should never pressure you to weaken your computer’s security so you can proceed.

PROMPTSPY gives Android users a good reason to pay attention to where apps come from. Google says Play Protect checks apps for harmful behavior. It also scans apps installed from outside Google Play. Keep Play Protect enabled. Be especially cautious with sideloaded apps from websites, messages or unfamiliar app stores. The same thinking applies to browser extensions. An extension can gain significant access to what happens inside your browser, so install only what you need from a source you trust.

A password manager helps you create unique passwords for your accounts. It can also give you a useful phishing warning. If a saved password normally fills automatically and suddenly does not, stop and check the website address before typing the password yourself. Use multifactor authentication where available. Better yet, use a passkey when a service supports one. Keep in mind that some information-stealing malware can target browser cookies or authenticated sessions. MFA still helps, but no login protection gives you permission to ignore malware on the device itself.

Back up anything you would hate to lose. That could include family photos and financial records. Keep other irreplaceable files covered too. A cloud backup can help. An external drive that you disconnect when you are finished backing up can give you another recovery option. A backup will not stop malware from stealing data, but it can make ransomware or destructive malware much less devastating.

Watch for unfamiliar programs and unexplained security alerts. Pay attention if your antivirus suddenly turns itself off or your browser starts behaving strangely. If you think a computer may be infected, disconnect it from the internet and run a trusted security scan. For a PC, you can follow our guide on what to do if you think your PC has a virus. If passwords or financial information may have been exposed, use a different trusted device to change important passwords. Then sign out of active sessions where the service allows it. Check your financial accounts for activity you do not recognize. Act quickly if something looks wrong.
Kurt’s key takeaways

PROMPTFLUX caught my attention because of what it says about the direction malware is taking. For years, attackers have found ways to change malicious code and make detection harder. AI gives them another tool for doing that while the malware is running. I would not take that to mean antivirus protection suddenly became obsolete. Strong security software already looks beyond a simple malware fingerprint. Behavior monitoring and cloud-based analysis can help catch threats that have never been seen before.

What concerns me more is how quickly the technology is progressing. PROMPTFLUX was experimental. PROMPTSTEAL appeared in live operations. PROMPTSPY showed how AI could help malware interpret an Android interface. Now Google is seeing attackers use agentic AI to automate larger portions of an attack. For me, the lesson is pretty straightforward. Do not depend on one security feature to save you. Keep good protection running, take security warnings seriously and make it difficult for malicious software to get onto your devices in the first place. If something does get through, reacting quickly can limit how far the damage goes.

As malware becomes capable of changing its code and making more decisions with AI, do you think security companies can stay ahead, or are we heading toward a point where it becomes much harder to know whether our devices are truly safe? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: 3 VPN settings to check before your next trip
summary: Your VPN may quietly drop protection when switching between airport Wi-Fi and hotel Wi-Fi. Key settings like auto-connect and kill switch help.
story: Travel expert Lee Abbamonte discusses the risks posed by fraudulent wireless connections on commercial flights and what passengers should check before accessing the internet in the air.

Has this happened to you? You're at the airport, connected to the terminal Wi-Fi, VPN running and feeling good about your security. You board, put your phone in airplane mode, land a few hours later and switch airplane mode off. Your phone finds the hotel Wi-Fi. You open your email and start scrolling.

What you probably didn't notice is the moment in between. For a few seconds, your phone may have been reconnecting while your VPN was still catching up. During that brief window, some traffic could have left your device without VPN protection.

Most websites today use HTTPS encryption, so losing your VPN for a few seconds does not mean everything you do suddenly becomes visible. Still, a VPN adds another layer of privacy, particularly when you are connecting to airport, hotel and coffee shop networks you do not control. Here's how you can reduce those connection gaps while traveling.

HOW TO STREAM SAFELY WHILE TRAVELING OUTSIDE THE US
Using auto-connect and a kill switch can help keep your VPN protection in place when you move between hotel, airport and other travel networks. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Why switching networks can interrupt your VPN

A VPN works by building an encrypted tunnel between your device and the internet. While that tunnel is active, your connection to the VPN server is encrypted. However, the VPN relies on an internet connection. When your phone drops one network and connects to another, the VPN may need to re-establish that tunnel.

Usually, this happens so quickly that you barely notice. However, a weak signal, slow hotel login page or network that takes a few extra seconds to connect can create a brief period when your device has internet access before the VPN reconnects.

This can happen during completely ordinary activities. You might switch from cellular data to airport Wi-Fi after landing. Later, your phone may move from the airport network to your hotel's Wi-Fi. The same thing can happen when your phone wakes from sleep in a new location or reconnects after losing cellular service. For travelers who move between networks frequently, those transitions are worth paying attention to.
What happens when your VPN is disconnected

When your VPN is disconnected, websites and online services can generally see the public IP address assigned by your internet provider or Wi-Fi network instead of the VPN server's IP address. That address can reveal information such as your approximate location and internet provider.

A VPN also helps prevent the operator of a Wi-Fi network from easily seeing details about the internet services your device is contacting. Most trusted websites and apps already encrypt sensitive traffic using HTTPS or other encryption. That greatly reduces what someone monitoring a public Wi-Fi connection can see.

However, risks remain if you connect to a fake or compromised Wi-Fi network. Someone controlling the network may try to direct you to a fraudulent login page, interfere with your connection or exploit websites and apps that are not properly encrypted.

A VPN adds another layer of protection by encrypting traffic between your device and the VPN server and masking your normal public IP address. A kill switch can provide an additional safeguard by preventing internet traffic from leaving your device if the VPN unexpectedly disconnects.
1) Turn on VPN auto-connect
The first setting to check is auto-connect. Most VPN apps offer some form of automatic connection. Without it, your VPN may stay disconnected until you remember to open the app and turn it back on.

After a long flight, a trip through baggage claim and the rush to reach your hotel, that can be easy to forget. With auto-connect enabled, your VPN can attempt to restore its connection automatically when your device gets back online or joins a new network. Check your VPN app before traveling and make sure its automatic connection options are configured the way you want them.
THE TRICK TO SMOOTHER STREAMING AT HOME AND ON THE ROAD
Travelers using hotel or public Wi-Fi may benefit from a VPN's added privacy, though it cannot overcome an overloaded network. (Photo by Alex Pantling/Getty Images)
2) Enable your VPN kill switch

The second setting to check is the kill switch. A VPN kill switch is designed to block internet traffic if your VPN unexpectedly disconnects. That helps prevent your device from simply falling back to an unprotected connection while the VPN is trying to reconnect.

However, kill switches do not all work exactly the same way. Some protect you only when the VPN connection unexpectedly drops. Others can be configured to block internet access whenever the VPN is not connected.
Android users may also have system-level options such as Always-on VPN and Block connections without VPN, depending on their device and VPN provider.

Some reputable VPN services also offer additional kill switch options on supported platforms. Keep in mind that stronger settings that block all traffic outside the VPN can interfere with local network features or internet access when the VPN is intentionally turned off. The important thing is to understand how your VPN's kill switch works before you depend on it while traveling.

There is one situation that can complicate things: the captive portal. That's the webpage airports, hotels and other public Wi-Fi networks sometimes require you to open before they grant internet access. You may need to accept terms, enter a room number or complete another login step.
Because your device does not yet have normal internet access, the VPN may not be able to connect until you finish that process. Strict kill switch settings can occasionally make this more difficult.

If you encounter a Wi-Fi login page, complete the network's sign-in process and then confirm that your VPN is connected before opening email, financial accounts or other sensitive services. Also make sure you are joining the correct Wi-Fi network. If you are uncertain, ask an airport employee, hotel staff member or business employee for the official network name.
3) Choose a VPN protocol that reconnects quickly

Settings help, but reconnection speed also depends on the underlying technology your VPN uses. This is known as the VPN protocol. Different VPN protocols handle network changes in different ways. Some are particularly well suited to phones and laptops that frequently move between Wi-Fi and cellular connections. For the best VPN software, see my expert review of the best VPNs for browsing the web privately on your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.
WHY YOUR VPN KEEPS GETTING BLOCKED AND THE SIMPLE FIX
Using an always-on VPN or your phone’s hotspot can help protect sensitive work accounts while traveling. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
A quick VPN checklist for travelers
Before your next trip, take a minute to check your VPN:

Turn on auto-connect so the VPN can attempt to reconnect when your device joins a new network.Enable the kill switch and understand exactly what it blocks when the VPN disconnects.Choose a VPN protocol designed for fast reconnection, or use your VPN provider's recommended automatic setting.Verify the official Wi-Fi network name before joining public Wi-Fi.Complete any required airport or hotel Wi-Fi login page, then confirm your VPN is connected before accessing sensitive accounts.
Turn on auto-connect so the VPN can attempt to reconnect when your device joins a new network.
Enable the kill switch and understand exactly what it blocks when the VPN disconnects.
Choose a VPN protocol designed for fast reconnection, or use your VPN provider's recommended automatic setting.
Verify the official Wi-Fi network name before joining public Wi-Fi.
Complete any required airport or hotel Wi-Fi login page, then confirm your VPN is connected before accessing sensitive accounts.

You should also test your setup before leaving home. Connect to your VPN, turn Wi-Fi off and switch to cellular data. Then turn Wi-Fi back on and watch what your VPN does. Does it reconnect automatically? Does the kill switch block traffic while the VPN is disconnected? How long does the connection take to return? A quick test can help you catch a setting that needs attention before you are relying on your VPN in an airport or hotel.
Kurt's key takeaways

Most websites already use HTTPS encryption, so a brief VPN interruption does not leave all of your online activity exposed. Still, a VPN provides another valuable layer of privacy when you are using networks you do not control. The biggest issue for travelers is making sure the VPN actually reconnects when a phone or laptop moves between cellular service, airport Wi-Fi, hotel Wi-Fi and other networks. Turn on auto-connect, understand how your kill switch works and use a protocol that handles network changes efficiently. A few minutes spent checking your settings before a trip can help keep your VPN connection more consistent while you are on the move.
Have you ever noticed your VPN disconnect when switching networks, or is there a setting you use to keep it connected while traveling? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: His home changed hands for $5. Could it happen to your family?
summary: A South Carolina caregiver allegedly gained power of attorney over a 75-year-old with Parkinson's, then transferred his home via quitclaim deed for $5.
story: A woman caught up in a two-year LinkedIn romance scam that used a real man's identity shares the tactics a scammer used to build trust and trick her into sending nearly $1 million.

A deed can change hands without a burglar breaking a window or a scammer hacking a computer. Sometimes the first warning signs are sitting inside county records, bank accounts and email inboxes, waiting for someone to notice.

A disturbing case out of South Carolina shows why families may want to put a few digital safeguards in place now. According to a local report, a daughter says her 75-year-old father, who had Parkinson's disease and a brain injury, became increasingly isolated after a caregiver entered his life.

Within weeks, the caregiver was named as his power of attorney. A quitclaim deed later transferred his Conway home to her for $5. His daughter also says bank statements show money moving from his account to the caregiver, including after his death. Conway police said they were investigating.

The allegations have not been proven in court. Still, the case raises a question every family with an aging or vulnerable loved one should consider: Would you know if someone changed a deed, moved money or took control of an important account? Technology cannot prevent every form of financial exploitation. However, the right alerts can create an early-warning system that makes major changes much harder to hide.
