Fox News Digital has reached out to the Saudi Embassy in Washington, D.C., for comment.
Fox News Digital’s Efrat Lachter contributed to this report.
Greg Norman is a reporter at Fox News Digital.

title: Family member of lawyer who coined 'genocide' seeks to strip name from group accusing Israel of atrocity
summary: A relative of "genocide" term creator Raphael Lemkin wants a Pennsylvania nonprofit to drop the family name over its accusations against Israel. The institute defends its mission and name.
story: Calvary Chapel Chino Hills Pastor Jack Hibbs decries those who call Israel’s war in Gaza a genocide on ‘Fox News @ Night.’

A family member of Raphael Lemkin, a Jewish lawyer who escaped Europe during World War II and coined the term "genocide," is in a fight to have his name removed from a Pennsylvania nonprofit organization that accuses Israel of the exact term he came up with.

The Lemkin Institute for Genocide Prevention and Human Security has "warned of genocide in Gaza since Oct. 13, 2023," less than a week after Hamas terror attacks killed about 1,200 and resulted in the capture of 251 hostages in 2023.

On Oct. 28, 2023, the institute issued a "statement of mourning for the Gazans and the world," saying that "these two major military powers [the U.S. and Israel] are committing genocide in Gaza only weeks after actively enabling genocide against another besieged people: the Armenians of Artsakh." It also warned that "if the world allows these two powers to continue to act with this level of impunity, genocide will become the normative policy of both dictatorships and the world’s so-called democracies alike."
PROMINENT HOLOCAUST MUSEUM CHALLENGES MAMDANI WITH OFFER IN RESPONSE TO CLAIMS ABOUT 'GENOCIDE' IN GAZA
International lawyer Raphael Lemkin helped draft the Genocide Convention, which maps out prevention and punishment for the crime of genocide. (Getty Images)

The man calling for the change is Joseph Lemkin — whose father was Raphael’s cousin — and the sole survivor after his family of six was killed during the Holocaust. Joseph told Fox News Digital that growing up the son of a Holocaust survivor meant being followed by "a black cloud" that colored his entire life.

In one example, he explained that when the families at his Jewish day school placed ads during an annual banquet to celebrate their successes, his father wrote a yearly commemoration of the memories of his more than 40 family members who died during the Holocaust, including his parents and brother killed at Auschwitz and two brothers who died after joining underground resistance groups.
He said his father raised funds for the impoverished Raphael’s funeral when he died in 1959, and worked until weeks before his death to fundraise for the betterment of his fellow Jewish Americans.

Joseph’s experience as the child of a Holocaust survivor came to mind again when his teenage son showed him a social media post from the Lemkin Institute using the family name to accuse Israel of genocide.
"Seeing the impact and how my son came across it made me really more concerned about it," Lemkin said.
ANTI-ISRAEL NONPROFIT UNDER FEDERAL INVESTIGATION OVER FINANCIAL DEALINGS: REPORT
Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro speaks during a re-election campaign kickoff event in Philadelphia on Jan. 8, 2026. (Rachel Wisniewski/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

In an effort to keep the family name from being "turned on its head," he said he has worked with the European Jewish Association (EJA) to submit a letter of complaint to the office of Democratic Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro and to Pennsylvania’s Department of State’s Bureau of Corporations and Charitable Organizations. In June, Lemkin and his team also sent out letters referencing their concerns to other leaders in Pennsylvania.

In response to a request from Shapiro’s office for additional information, Lemkin and the EJA submitted a 32-page comprehensive legal submission and statement of facts and a 58-page evidentiary appendix in April 2025. He said he believes that an investigation has been opened into the complaint.

Pennsylvania's Department of State spokesman, Geoff Morrow, told Fox News Digital "the Department [of State] cannot confirm or deny whether any organization has had a complaint filed against it or is under investigation."
Gov. Shapiro’s office did not respond to requests for comment from Fox News Digital.
ISRAEL TURNS TABLES ON UN OFFICIAL CLAIMING 'GENOCIDE' IN GAZA WITH BASIC QUESTIONS
People walk through Times Square as they participate in a pro-Palestinian rally on Oct. 4, 2025, in New York City. (Stephanie Keith/Getty Images)

In an Oct. 13, 2025, press release responding to an op-ed, the Lemkin Institute stated, "It is very hard to imagine that Raphael Lemkin would not have seen the genocidal dynamics of the present conflict early on, given his definition of the term and his historical studies. We share Raphael Lemkin’s belief in the need for a Jewish national home, but that has not meant that we are unable to see the genocide before our eyes."

The same press release also noted, "Joseph Lemkin does not speak for the entire Lemkin family, nor does he officially represent a Lemkin estate. We have Lemkin family members on our side who reached out to us after October 7, 2023. Peter Lemkin, in whose childhood home Raphael Lemkin was a frequent visitor, has been particularly supportive, offering encouragement, sharing insights into Lemkin’s work, and informing us of his family's close collaboration in the effort to get the Genocide Convention ratified by states."

In a statement to Fox News Digital, the institute again questioned Joseph’s representation of Raphael, stating in part, "Over the years, members of the Lemkin family have reached out to express their support for our work. Joseph Lemkin has expressed his disagreement with our work. There is no legal battle between the Lemkin Institute and the Lemkin family."
Peter Lemkin did not respond to Fox News Digital’s requests for comment. Nor did another family member identified to Fox News Digital by the institute as being supportive of its work.

The statement to Fox News Digital continued, "The Institute was founded in 2016/2017. In 2021, it was renamed to honor the life and work of Raphael Lemkin, whose research and moral commitments, reflected not only in the 1948 Genocide Convention but also in the many case studies he completed before his untimely death at age 59, have deeply influenced the work of the Institute's founders. Since Raphael Lemkin died without heirs or an estate, there was no official representative for the Lemkin family to contact for permission," it stated.
Anti-Israel activists protest outside the United Nations headquarters in New York, on April 7, 2025. (Selcuk Acar/Anadolu via Getty Images)

The statement also noted, "The Lemkin Institute for Genocide Prevention is an all-volunteer organization founded to fill the gaps in genocide prevention that co-founders Dr. Elisa von Joeden-Forgey and Dr. Irene Massimino observed during several visits to Northern Iraq in 2016 and 2017, when they met with religious leaders, government officials, and survivors of ISIS genocide, including Yezidi, Christians, Shabak-Shia, Kakay and other religious, national, and ethnic minorities."

It continued, "This includes, of course, security for the Jewish people, who continue to be the targets of one of the oldest and most lethal global genocidal ideologies — antisemitism. This also includes Palestinians, Darfuris, Armenians, Artsakhsis, Rohingya, Ukrainians, Uighurs, Amhara, trans people, Yezidis, many Christian populations, many Muslim populations, Somalilanders, Kurds, the Karakalpak, many Black and Native communities in the Western Hemisphere, and far too many other groups to mention here. Our world is unfortunately awash in genocide and it benefits all humanity for all of us to be involved in preventing the crime."
UN COMMISSION ACCUSES ISRAEL OF 'EXTERMINATION' IN CONTROVERSIAL REPORT

A participant wrapped in a flag of Israel stands at the main gate with the lettering "Arbeit macht frei" (Work sets you free) at the start of the annual March of The Living to commemorate the victims of the Holocaust during World War II, at the memorial site of the former Auschwitz-Birkenau Nazi death camp in Oswiecim, Poland, on April 14, 2026. (Wojtek Radwanski/AFP via Getty Images)

The institute utilized the October 2025 press release to start a fundraising campaign "to cover urgent legal fees, hire a full-time administrator, and ensure the survival of the Lemkin Institute." They stated that "the attempt to discredit us or to shut down our work is part of a wider effort to silence opposition to Israel’s genocide in the USA. But we will not allow our work to be smeared, or our voices to be silenced."

Israeli civil rights attorney and president of the Shurat HaDin Law Center, Nitsana Darshan-Leitner, who is not party to the dispute, told Fox News Digital, "The real question is not simply ‘standing,’ but whether the Institute has a lawful right to use Raphael Lemkin’s name in a manner that implies his endorsement, his family’s authorization, or fidelity to his beliefs. The Institute apparently never received permission from Lemkin, his estate, or an authorized representative when it appropriated the name. While using a deceased scholar’s name is not automatically unlawful, it becomes legally actionable when it misleads donors and the public, creates a false impression of endorsement, constitutes deceptive charitable solicitation, or appropriates the reputation and goodwill attached to that individual’s identity."

The main entrance at the former Nazi death camp of Auschwitz, and, right, Raphael Lemkin, who helped draft the convention that maps out prevention and punishment for the crime of genocide. (AP Photo/Markus Schreiber/Getty Images)

Commenting recently on the growing threat of antisemitism worldwide after the Hamas attacks of Oct. 7, 2023, renowned historian Sir Simon Schama called accusations that Israel has committed genocide in Gaza a "blood libel" in his keynote address at the Holocaust Educational Trust on Sept. 7. Schama stated, "We, the victims of the greatest genocide the world has ever seen, are being called perpetrators of genocide."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The Lemkin Institute has published multiple reports on the Israel-Gaza war that allege genocide by Israel. On May 28, 2024, they wrote, "Even if there were legitimate doubts about Israel’s genocide, there is no doubt that Israel is committing atrocity crimes of the most barbaric kind. Israel must be stopped."

The institute also said it is "disgusted by Western leaders, especially in the USA, Germany, and the U.K. They have demonstrated not only that they don’t care one bit about genocide prevention and human rights, but also that they are willing to allow an ally to commit atrocity crimes while they offer material and diplomatic support." The Lemkin Institute suggested that "they should also be put on trial."
Beth Bailey writes on the United Nations, worldwide antisemitism, and regions in conflict for Fox News.

title: New campaign aims to help millions at risk of losing Medicaid coverage under work requirements
summary: On Jan. 1, new federal work and reporting requirements kick in for Medicaid, leaving millions at risk of losing healthcare coverage as states scramble to prepare for the most substantial change to the program in decades.
story: MECHANICSVILLE, Va. — In 100 days, on Jan. 1, new federal work and reporting requirements kick in for Medicaid recipients, leaving roughly 10 million Americans at risk of losing healthcare coverage, as states scramble to prepare for the most substantial change to the program in decades.

A new, $2 million campaign called “Keep Your Care,” an independent nonprofit, launched Wednesday. Shared exclusively with NBC News, it aims to educate states and Medicaid recipients ahead of the massive change.

For Melanie and Greg Stephens, who live in a small town outside of Richmond, Virginia, the resources can’t come soon enough. On Aug. 31, the family received a letter in the mail informing them of the new guidelines.
“When I received the letter about all the changes coming up, I had a panic attack because I was like, ‘Oh, my gosh, what does this mean?’” Melanie Stephens said.
New Medicaid work requirements could put caregivers at risk of losing coverage

As full-time caregivers for their disabled daughter, Rachel, they are exempt from the 80-hours-per-month work or community service requirement that will affect most eligible adults in the new year. But they will still need to prove they are exempt every six months.

“Our concern is not so much on our part because we are thorough,” Greg Stephens said. “Once it leaves us and goes to a Medicaid worker to process, that’s where we are concerned they’re going to miss a deadline or fall through the cracks, and we have no control over that.”

The work requirements, supported by Republicans to address wasteful spending, were passed as part of the “big, beautiful bill” signed into law by President Donald Trump last year. But they could leave eligible recipients without coverage because of the administrative hoops they will now have to jump through, health care advocates argue.
Virginia Health Secretary Marvin Figueroa, in an interview with NBC News, described it as “fighting government for something that you’re entitled to.”

“I go back to just look at the debate that allowed this bill to pass. This is a predictable surprise,” he added. “The discussion was about losing coverage, and I think we’re going to see that across the board.”

Senate Majority Leader John Thune and many Republicans defended the cuts at the time, arguing they were “targeting waste, fraud, and abuse in the program” and also “want to make sure that this doesn’t hurt beneficiaries.”

“And what’s being said out there by the Democrats is totally inaccurate,” Thune said in an interview last year, days before his chamber voted to pass the legislation. “It doesn’t cut Medicaid … What we’re talking about here is getting rid of waste, fraud and abuse, strengthening and improving the program for the people who need it the most and for whom it was intended, and really making this program more solvent for the long term.”

Keep Your Care was established by two health care advocacy groups, Caring Across Generations and the Healthcare Education Project, and the Service Employees International Union. The group’s state-level work will focus on Georgia, North Carolina, Illinois, Michigan, California, Virginia and New York, states with Medicaid expansion under the Affordable Care Act where millions stand to lose coverage. The group is working with communities to help eligible Americans maintain coverage, and influence state and local governments on how the new requirements are implemented. Its website will list state-specific information about what is changing, determine the requirements and exemptions that may apply and track reporting deadlines.

Greg Stephens admitted that, as a physician, he judged patients who were covered by Medicaid until he became a recipient himself. But his daughter Rachel, 22, has faced increasing health challenges since Covid and requires 24/7 management: so much so that he quit his job last year, just as his wife had years before. With no income on paper, they had to apply for Medicaid.

“We spent months calling other insurance companies and other agents and trying to find another way, and there was no other way,” Melanie Stephens shared during an interview at their home, accomplished because Rachel’s grandparents looked after her during the 30-minute window.

The coverage allows the Stephens to care for Rachel, who is bound to a wheelchair, at home, which also means administering medications five times per day and feeding her through a tube. Rachel’s care is so complex that the only other option for their daughter, the Stephens said, would be an institution.
“There’s no one that could possibly care for her medically, or emotionally or cognitively,” the Stephens shared, adding: “She would have no will to live.”

The Stephens acknowledged that while there may be some individuals on Medicaid who could work, the changes made were an overcorrection, burdening eligible families with unnecessary stress and paperwork.
“There’s a lot of people that are getting health care through Medicaid expansion, like ourselves, that absolutely need this exclusion to be able to do what we do,” Greg Stephens said.

title: We want to hear about your experience with Tricare medical coverage
summary: If you receive healthcare through the military benefits program, or if you are a Tricare employee or contractor, share your story.
story: Tricare promises to provide health benefits to millions of active-duty service members, veterans and their families.

But in recent months, NBC News has uncovered a slew of complaints about the U.S. military’s healthcare program as part of our “Cost of Denial” series, which examines coverage refusals and other insurance-related problems.
Many people who receive healthcare through Tricare say their issues began when the military switched the companies that administer the program at the start of 2025.

After NBC News reported on one veteran whose claims were repeatedly denied, delaying crucial care after his cancer diagnosis, one of the contracted companies issued a public apology, and Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton opened an investigation into denied claims.

We are continuing to cover Tricare and want to hear about people’s experiences. If you are a Tricare beneficiary, provider, contractor or employee dealing with denied claims, delayed reimbursements or other issues, we would like to hear from you.

title: Supreme Court declines to intervene in custody case involving newborn with heart condition
summary: The Supreme Court declined to get involved in the case of a surrogate enmeshed in a multistate custody battle with California parents who at one point asked her to abort the fetus because of a heart defect.
story: Justice Elena Kagan on Tuesday rejected a request for the Supreme Court to get involved in the case of a surrogate enmeshed in a multistate custody battle with California parents who at one point asked her to abort the fetus because of a heart defect.

McKenna West gave birth to the couple’s baby in Texas last month and argued in court there that California denied her due process when it awarded custody of the child, whom she named Gabriel, to his genetic parents.
A Texas judge dismissed her claims. She then appealed to the Supreme Court. Kagan denied to issue a stay in the case in a Tuesday order with no written decision.

In a filing earlier this month, attorneys for West urged Kagan, who handles emergency matters involving California, to intervene because a “life hangs in the balance.” They said West is concerned that Gabriel might not get the medical care he needs if he remains in the custody of his parents, Omar Ahmed and Nausheen Gilkar.

Gilkar told a judge in Dallas last month that she and her husband were dedicated to getting the son they named Rumi the help he requires — and that the “unstable” West is making an already tragic situation more fraught.
“She’s making us run from doctor to doctor, state to state with our baby. She’s trying to take him,” Gilkar testified.

The Texas Supreme Court issued a ruling last week allowing the baby to be moved to California, where the parents have medical care for the child lined up, the Texas Tribune reported. “Sustaining the life of the medically fragile child is the paramount concern in this time-sensitive matter,” the ruling said.

The baby was born with hypoplastic left heart syndrome, a congenital defect in which one side of the organ is underdeveloped, preventing normal blood flow. The condition can quickly become fatal if it is left untreated.
According to court documents obtained last month by The Associated Press, the newborn was in critical condition and “suffering from potential complications” following heart surgery in Texas.

The parents had turned to surrogacy after efforts involving in vitro fertilization treatments failed. They signed a contract in August 2025 with West — a cardiac nurse who was living in Anchorage, Alaska — that included a clause stipulating the pregnancy could be terminated if there was a “fetal abnormality.”

West said the parents tried to invoke the clause after the heart defect was diagnosed, but she refused to comply. She ultimately headed to Texas, where her case was championed by state Attorney General Ken Paxton, the Republican nominee for a U.S. Senate seat this fall.

With Paxton’s assistance, West got an order directing that the newborn get necessary lifesaving care in Texas after he was born. The parents had planned for him to get that care in their native California.
Judges in Alaska and Texas ultimately deferred to the California ruling, according to West’s Supreme Court filing.
West alleges that Ahmed and Gilkar violated their surrogacy agreement by seeking custody in California. She said the agreement had called for any legal challenges to be heard in Alaska.
West contended that the California decision should be tossed out because she did not get proper due process, and she said she is being kept in the dark about the baby’s health.
In a court filing, West said that “without relief, she will receive no further information about the child she carried for 37 weeks and fought to save.”
The parents’ attorney said that they are focused on the baby’s health and that West is engaged in “political theater.”

title: Capt. Sully Sullenberger speaks out about Alzheimer’s diagnosis: ‘I’ve done harder things’
summary: For the first time since announcing his Alzheimer’s diagnosis over the summer, Capt. Sully Sullenberger discusses the impact on his life.
story: For the first time since announcing his Alzheimer’s diagnosis over the summer, Capt. Chesley “Sully” Sullenberger has discussed his experience with the disease and what lies ahead.

“I’ve done harder things than this before,” Sullenberger, the  retired pilot who successfully landed a commercial airliner filled with passengers on the Hudson River in 2009, told “Good Morning America” on Wednesday.
Sullenberger, 75, and his wife, Lorrie Sullenberger, spoke to host Robin Roberts about the diagnosis, which he revealed in a post on his website in July.

“I recently found out I have been diagnosed with Alzheimer’s Disease. It is early stage,” Sullenberger wrote in the July 14 post. “For now, this means a name may not come easily to me, I forget a story I have recently told, or I don’t sleep as well, but I am in the beginning of this long journey.”

Sullenberger became a household name when he successfully landed a commercial airplane in the Hudson River, saving everyone on board, after a bird strike caused both engines to fail shortly after takeoff. The act has since been known as “The Miracle on the Hudson.”
Clint Eastwood dramatized Sullenberger’s heroic exploits in the 2016 film “Sully,” starring Tom Hanks in the titular role.
Roberts on Wednesday asked Sullenberger to compare his diagnosis to that heroic moment.

“We had to devise a plan, execute that plan flawlessly for the first time — never having done it before — and save every life in 208 seconds,” Sullenberger recalled. He added, “had even one person not survived, I would have considered it a tragic failure.”

“So I think we’re we’re doing the same thing here,” he continued of his diagnosis. “We’re focusing clearly on the highest priority items first, and we are ignoring everything we don’t have time to do.”

Sullenberger is receiving monthly treatments for the disease, which aims to slow the condition. Both he and his wife said initially, they wanted to keep his diagnosis private, but later decided to speak out with the hope that they could help others.
“This is a disease, not a character flaw,” Lorrie Sullenberger said.  “I think we need to talk about it more openly, and maybe other people can do the same.”
Sullenberger added that at first, he questioned: “Why me?”
But, “we’re not by any means alone,” he reflected. “We’re part of this community who are trying to make the best of a bad situation.”
Sullenberger said the first signs of the disease were forgetting things that he normally wouldn’t, like people’s names — even those he has known for a long time — and events.
The symptoms were easy to dismiss in the beginning, his wife said, because they were so minor. She noted that what a lot of people see in the news are cases of late-stage Alzheimer’s disease.
“If you have doubts, get tested because the sooner you act, the more options there are, the better the outcome is likely to be,” Sullenberger said.
One of the couple’s daughters, Kelly Sullenberger, told Roberts that since her dad’s diagnosis, her priority has been spending more time with their family.
“Our family likes to be prepared and have plans in place. It runs in our blood, and it’s something that you can’t really plan for,” she said.
Sullenberger, who is set to be inducted into the National Aviation Hall of Fame this month, told Roberts that his greatest concern is “that this is my last flight.”
“But if this has to be my last flight,” he said, “I’m going to go out using full afterburner.”

title: Netflix turns Willy Wonka’s chocolate factory into a real-life ‘social experiment’
summary: Lickable wallpaper.
story: Lickable wallpaper. An edible garden replete with gummy foliage. A chocolate river made of 25,000 gallons of chocolate goop.
Nods to the “Willy Wonka & the Chocolate Factory” films appear everywhere in Netflix’s new reality competition show “Wonka’s The Golden Ticket.”

But the show, which debuted on the streamer Wednesday, also embraces the darker elements of Roald Dahl’s 1964 children’s book and subsequent films. Unlike the original story, which ultimately rewards protagonist Charlie for his humility and lack of greed after a tour of Wonka’s whimsical chocolate factory, Netflix’s series incentivizes contestants to scheme and strategize to win a $3 million prize.

“This is the modern-day take on the movie, so we weren’t really ever trying to be the morality police. We never ever wanted to set out to be the producers that dictated who behaved well and who behaved poorly,” said showrunner Emer Harkin. “Because let’s be real, we’re all human. We all make mistakes. We all misbehave. We seek redemption. We all have our inflected storylines, and so that was important for us.”

Yet when the trailer dropped earlier this year, fans of the pop culture classic appeared less preoccupied with the reality twist on the story than with another creative choice: the use of generative AI to replicate the late Gene Wilder’s voice from the original 1971 film.

“A whole new generation of real-life Golden Ticket holders will compete for a life-changing prize or say a most unfortunate goodbye,” the AI-generated voice of Wilder says in the series. “Marvel at the magic you remember and delight in my newest wonders beyond imagination. The most extraordinary competition on Earth is about to begin.”

The decision is one that Harkin and co-showrunner Alison Holloway stand behind, saying the use of Wilder’s likeness meant to honor him, not diminish his legacy. It was done with explicit approval, and encouragement, from his estate and wife.

“The more we developed the series, the more we kept thinking: What would Wonka do at this point? What would Wonka say? i.e., What would Gene Wilder say?” Holloway said. “So it became clear to us that Gene Wilder was perhaps the only voice that could do this.”
No in-person hosts appear in the show, but the disembodied AI-generated replica of Wilder’s voice floats in every so often to announce new challenges and contestant terminations.
The emerging use of generative AI in Hollywood has stirred pushback from film industry workers, who say they’re worried about loss of labor in an already dismal market for entertainment jobs.

When the “Wonka” reality show trailer was released, some fans online suggested that Wilder wouldn’t have signed off on the project if he were alive today, pointing to how he criticized the 2005 “Wonka” remake.
Holloway said she understands and shares people’s concerns over AI use. But receiving support from Wilder’s widow, Karen Boyer, made her feel at peace with the decision to proceed with the idea.

“I think we have to believe that the people who loved him the most want this to happen,” Holloway said. “And of course, it’s out of total respect for his legacy that we’ve gone to such lengths to get it as best as we can.”

In order for the show to capture the cadence, the tone and the “whimsy” of Wilder’s voice, the team behind the show sifted through hours of Wilder’s audiobooks, which Boyer provided to them. Netflix partnered with the AI voice generation company ElevenLabs, which has been making inroads in Hollywood in recent years collaborating with both studios and celebrities.
To bring the fictional world to life, Netflix employed a team of working magicians to make the “magic” feel real to the contestants.

The competitors, who earned their entry onto the show by finding a golden ticket hidden within a Wonka-themed chocolate bar, arrive at the giant chocolate factory to face off in a phantasmagoria of dramatic candy-colored challenges.

In the first challenge of the show, some contestants disappeared in a puff of fog while sitting right beside their partners — extracting reactions that the showrunners said “had to be absolutely authentic.”

“We watched that movie over and over and over again, and it gave us the template for the 2026 social experiment,” Holloway said. “We hope we’ve captured all the nostalgia … the magic that was always there, the unpredictability that was always there, the sort of darkness that was always there.”

title: CNN, Politico and MS NOW to face off with Trump administration in court over White House ban
summary: The news outlets that President Donald Trump abruptly banned from accessing the White House will be in court Wednesday to argue the policy is unconstitutional.
story: The trio of media outlets that President Donald Trump abruptly banned from accessing the White House will be in court Wednesday to argue their expulsion was unconstitutional and should be lifted immediately.

“This ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles,” lawyers for CNN, Politico and MS NOW said in a court filing Monday ahead of the hearing.
“The ban is unconstitutional and should be immediately restrained,” they contended, citing legal precedent in the District of Columbia and U.S. Supreme Court.
The news organizations are scheduled to make their case to U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly at a 3:30 p.m. ET hearing.

Late Tuesday, the Justice Department defended the ban in a court filing, arguing that Trump had decided the outlets “failed to maintain basic minimum ‘standards of professionalism and decorum expected of those given access to the White House Complex, including’ by ‘publishing sensitive or classified information.’”
The outlets’ “access to the White House is a privilege — not a right,” the filing said.

On Tuesday, the White House Press Office sent letters to the three outlets alleging their coverage involved “trafficking in verifiable falsehoods about national security and other issues, and publishing sensitive or classified information,” the department said in the filing. The letters also were filed in court.

The articles cited in the letters included reporting on the construction of the White House ballroom and its related military security complex, the status of munitions supplies being used in the Iran war, an alleged FBI leak investigation involving a journalist, and sanctions on Russia.

In the letters, the administration gave the organizations a deadline of 5 p.m. Friday to “contest this initial decision” to bar them from the White House or the decision “will be final,” the filing said.
The outlets did not immediately respond to NBC News’ requests for comment on the allegations in the filing.
Kelly was nominated to the bench by Trump in his first term but ruled against him in a similar case back in 2018, when the White House pulled press credentials from then-CNN reporter Jim Acosta.

In a post on Truth Social on Monday, Trump said Kelly is a “great judge” for the media outlets, and suggested he believes he’ll rule against his administration. “[A]s usual, we’ll go for appeal,” he wrote, “because Fake News people and publications that only write negatively” should not be “allowed access to the most important Office anywhere in the World.”
Trump also criticized the judge as “totally disloyal” in a separate post late Tuesday.
The three news organizations have pointed to similar remarks by Trump as proof they’re victims of impermissible “viewpoint discrimination.”
Trump announced the outlets’ ban from the White House in a Truth Social post Friday, and said it was “a result of their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!”
“Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow,” he added.

Responding to questions from a reporter in the Oval Office a short time later, Trump referred to it as “the ban on the free press.” “Very simple ban. I don’t want them in my office. I don’t want them here,” he said.
He said the policy was in response to “cumulative stories over the last few years.”

“They purposely write negative news. And they do that because they want to try and diminish the Republicans and a Republican administration,” he said. “If they could straighten themselves out, I’d love it,” he added.

The outlets’ suit said Trump’s “words leave no doubt that banning Plaintiffs from the White House is retaliation for their protected newsgathering and speech — retaliation that is intended to cow them into changing their reporting and threaten other journalists lest they suffer the same fate. That is a paradigmatic First Amendment violation” and “flatly unconstitutional.”
The ban has already impacted news coverage, the suit says.
CNN is a member of the five-network rotation “for the primary television pool (also called the network pool) and absorbs 20% of the costs associated with such coverage,” the suit says.

The pool covers “events and locations where there is limited physical space for journalists,” their court papers say, and for “most of what the President does each day, the pool is the only source of independent reporting, video, and photographs available to the press and the public.”

“When CNN is the designated network pooler, CNN’s crew supplies the video and audio of the events involving the President and other White House officials to the other four networks and, through them and through pool distribution arrangements, to news organizations and the public. Among the recipients of the pool material are the more than 1,000 local affiliate television stations across the United States that receive the pool feed through CNN.”
NBC, ABC, CBS and Fox News are the other members of the rotation.
MS NOW is a rotating member of the secondary pool, while Politico is a member of the rotating print pool.

CNN had been scheduled to be the pool camera Monday, and the other networks in the TV network pool jointly declined to step in and replace its coverage, resulting in Trump’s remarks at a ribbon-cutting ceremony at the White House being inaudible.
His remarks at the United Nations on Tuesday and alongside New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani at a press conference Monday were picked up by U.N. cameras and local news outlets, respectively.
Trump defended the bans in a social media statement Monday and added a new argument — that “fake news” is a national security issue.

“The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish. It is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS, something that has grown like Cancer in our beloved United States of America,” he wrote. “It is a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW!”

title: The U.S. economy before and after the Iran war, in five charts
summary: On Feb. 27, the day before the United States and Israel attacked Iran, the American economy was on a steady course to lower inflation and attain greater buying power.
story: On Feb. 27, the day before the United States and Israel attacked Iran, the American economy was on a steady course to lower inflation and attain greater buying power. Gas was cheap and interest rates were coming down.
Today, none of those things are true anymore. When it comes to the U.S. economy, there’s before the Iran war — and since.

Despite assurances from President Donald Trump as early as March that the war would prove a “short-term excursion,” the conflict is about to round its seventh month. On Tuesday, Trump suggested that a deal could arrive after November’s midterm elections.

The morass has short-circuited Trump’s ability to tout other, more positive economic developments during his second term. The Census Bureau reported last week that the median U.S. household income hit an all-time high in 2025, while the percentage of people in the U.S. living in poverty fell to its lowest level on record. The stock market has done well this year, and the unemployment rate remains low.

Yet, on balance, the negative news has served to obscure the good, both for individual consumers and the nation at large. Before the war, gas prices were just under $3 a gallon. Today they’re at approximately $4.50 on average. Diesel prices went from an average of $3.75 on Feb. 28 to an all-time high of more than $6.50 on Tuesday.
This has caused a domino effect in which inflation rose, then borrowing costs, then mortgage rates.

Surveys of consumer sentiment and presidential approval polls continue to drift lower even as household spending on extras such as travel and dining out remains steady. In March, 35% of respondents to an NBC News poll said Trump had helped the economy. By September, that figure had declined to just 26%.
The White House defended the president’s record in a statement to NBC News.

“President Trump has always been clear about temporary disruptions as a result of the Iran conflict, but the Trump administration has remained laser-focused delivering on the President’s long-term economic agenda on the home front,” White House spokesman Kush Desai said in a statement.

The changes wrought by the war are nevertheless unmistakable. With less than six weeks until the midterm elections, the charts below offer the clearest picture yet of the challenge the White House faces as it works to retain Republican control of Congress.
Gas and diesel prices

The major reason for inflation’s run-up has been higher energy prices, especially fuel. Prior to the war’s launch, average gas prices stood at just under $3 a gallon, while diesel prices were less than $4 a gallon. Today, gas is nearly $4.50 — its highest ever for late September — and diesel prices continue to set records, most recently hitting $6.52.

title: We want to hear about your experience with Tricare medical coverage
summary: If you receive healthcare through the military benefits program, or if you are a Tricare employee or contractor, share your story.
story: Tricare promises to provide health benefits to millions of active-duty service members, veterans and their families.

But in recent months, NBC News has uncovered a slew of complaints about the U.S. military’s healthcare program as part of our “Cost of Denial” series, which examines coverage refusals and other insurance-related problems.
Many people who receive healthcare through Tricare say their issues began when the military switched the companies that administer the program at the start of 2025.

After NBC News reported on one veteran whose claims were repeatedly denied, delaying crucial care after his cancer diagnosis, one of the contracted companies issued a public apology, and Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton opened an investigation into denied claims.

We are continuing to cover Tricare and want to hear about people’s experiences. If you are a Tricare beneficiary, provider, contractor or employee dealing with denied claims, delayed reimbursements or other issues, we would like to hear from you.

title: Republican candidates highlight healthcare in 2026, battling voter distrust
summary: Health care is shaping up to be a vulnerability for the GOP in the 2026 midterm elections, when Democrats hope to capture the House and Senate.
story: WASHINGTON — Facing a challenging re-election bid, seven-term Rep. Scott Perry, R-Pa., says he’s not surprised that voters distrust the Republican Party to improve their healthcare.

“I can’t say that Republicans have done much about it,” Perry told NBC News before the House left last week for a lengthy election recess. “We’ve even passed some things here, but they don’t make it anywhere in the Senate. So, you know, people want results, not talk.”

Healthcare is shaping up to be a vulnerability for the GOP in the 2026 midterm elections, when Democrats hope to capture the House and the Senate. According to this month’s NBC News poll, voters trust Democrats over Republicans on healthcare by 22 points. A New York Times-Siena College poll similarly found that likely voters preferred Democrats by 24 points on the issue.

Still, Republicans are leaning in and highlighting the issue, with many of them using populist rhetoric criticizing insurance and drug companies. The goal, according to three GOP strategists, is more about trying to narrow the Democratic advantage than expecting to win on the issue.

In ultracompetitive Michigan, Senate candidate Mike Rogers is running an ad inveighing against high prescription drug costs relative to Canada. Rogers, a former Republican congressman who is calling for price transparency rules for hospitals and insurers, held an event Saturday attacking Democratic rival Abdul El-Sayed’s “Medicare for All” proposal.

“I just can’t think of a more important issue to the people of Michigan than healthcare — their costs, their rising costs and how we get to the bottom of it,” Rogers said at the healthcare-focused event in Taylor. “He wants Medicare for all. I want Medicare for seniors. They’ve earned it, they’ve worked for it, let’s improve it, let’s get it going.”

In Iowa, Republican Senate candidate Ashley Hinson launched an ad in May saying “healthcare companies are ripping you off” and that she’s “working with President Trump to take on big insurance companies.”

In a New Jersey swing district, Republican Rep. Tom Kean is running an ad lamenting that too many families “suffer because of big insurance companies.” Kean, who missed four months of work in the House citing treatment for depression, touted his bill to boost Labor Department authority to enforce mental health rules for insurance plans.
Even in deep red Kansas, Republican Sen. Roger Marshall is running an ad that credits him for “standing up to big insurance.”

Democrats are blasting the $1 trillion in Medicaid spending cuts that Republicans passed on party lines in President Donald Trump’s “big, beautiful bill,” as well as a pot of Obamacare funding that Republicans successfully pushed to end last year. Those two moves are estimated to cause more than 10 million people in the U.S. to lose coverage or, for those on Affordable Care Act, pay more for insurance. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., has vowed to restore the Medicaid and ACA funds as Democrats’ top priority if they capture House control.

“When you scratch the surface, healthcare is always an important issue to voters. And it’s an issue to try to talk to swing women voters and other subgroups of swing voters,” said Republican pollster Bill McInturff, who co-conducts the NBC News poll with Democratic pollster Jeff Horwitt.

“Republicans need to make up a deficit with women voters, and when you ask women what they are most focused on, healthcare always scores very high,” McInturff said, while adding: “You don’t have to win an issue. You just have to compete on the issue.”

According to NBC News polling, Democrats have consistently led on healthcare since the early 1990s. Their edge topped 30 points in 2008, ahead of a blue wave, and it fell to as little as 7 points in 2010, a red wave year.

And while Republicans spent much of the last decade, including Trump’s first term, attempting to repeal or undo the ACA, the party has never coalesced around an alternative. The party has long favored curtailing healthcare funding to align with its support for tax cuts, a position that is coming into conflict with its growing reliance on working-class voters.

Hinson, Kean and Marshall all voted for the Medicaid cuts. All but Kean voted against resurrecting ACA money. Rogers, who left Congress in 2015, has not said whether he’d support reviving the ACA funds, and his campaign had no comment about how he’d vote on reversing Medicaid cuts in Trump’s megabill last year.

“Michiganders see through Mike Rogers’ B.S. and understand that if he’s elected to the Senate, Rogers will eagerly continue his life’s work as Big Pharma’s greatest champion,” said Cole Wozniak, a spokesperson for El-Sayed, who has also vowed to restore the Medicaid and ACA money. “Michiganders deserve far better, which is why Dr. Abdul El-Sayed is running to fight back against Big Pharma and deliver Medicare for All.”

The White House’s internal polling shows that the administration’s work to lower drug prices is one of its most popular second term achievements, and it has encouraged Republican candidates to run on those issues, according to a senior White House official.

But when Trump held an event Friday to tout his most favored nation pricing policies for certain drugs under Medicaid, his message was drowned out by his just-announced decision to ban some news outlets from the White House.
Republicans who write healthcare legislation have also not made clear what they would do about healthcare if they maintain control of Congress.

Sen. Mike Crapo, R-Idaho, the chair of the Finance Committee that oversees healthcare policy, told NBC News his agenda next year will include “PBM fixes” — referring to third-party pharmacy benefit managers — and tackling “inefficiencies.”
Beyond that, he didn’t provide specifics.

“Our healthcare system is broken. I’m not going to tell you what the solutions are yet,” Crapo said. “So, I guess my response would be that we’re going to need to continue diving into the various issues from A to Z, and try to address the shortfalls and fix them. I think we’ve got a lot of good minds working on it.”

title: Defending Trump media ban, DOJ cites national security and says White House access is a ‘privilege’
summary: The Department of Justice said in a court filing late Tuesday that President Donald Trump has the right to ban media outlets CNN, MSNOW and Politico from the White House, calling their access a “privilege” and citing national security concerns.
story: The Department of Justice said in a court filing late Tuesday that President Donald Trump has the right to ban media outlets CNN, MSNOW and Politico from the White House, calling their access a “privilege” and citing national security concerns.
The filing urges a federal judge not to block the ban, ahead of a hearing Wednesday on the news organizations’ request for a temporary order restoring their access.
The Trump administration argues that the ban does not violate First Amendment protections on press freedom. “Access to the White House is a privilege—not a right,” the DOJ says in the filing.

It contends that the three news outlets had “failed to maintain basic minimum ‘standards of professionalism and decorum expected of those given access to the White House Complex,’ including, “publishing sensitive or classified information,” wrote DOJ Attorney Michael Velchik.

The DOJ said the three news organizations were sent individual letters from the White House Press Office earlier Tuesday laying out the reasoning for the revocation of their passes, and citing a “non-exhaustive list of reporting incidents” the White House said it had found “threatened national security and spread falsehoods.”
The letters cite stories on construction details related to the East Wing bunker, funding for the White House ballroom, munitions stockpiles impacted by the Iran war and sanctions against Russia.
The outlets did not immediately respond to overnight requests for comment from NBC News on the filing’s claims.
The letters give the news organizations a deadline of 5 p.m. on Friday to “contest this initial decision.” If the deadline is missed “this initial decision will be final,” they say.
Rubio defends White House media outlet ban
The decision to ban CNN, Politico and MS NOW came Friday via a Truth Social post, where Trump wrote that he was “proud to announce” the ban from the White House “effective immediately.”

He said the decision was “a result of their constant “reporting” FAKE NEWS! Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America.” He added: “Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow.”

Journalists from the three outlets, including MS NOW reporter Akayla Gardner, CNN’s Betsy Klein and Politico’s Cheyenne Haslett, subsequently found their access passes deactivated and their White House press credentials confiscated.
First Amendment experts and the White House Correspondents’ Association called the turning away of credentialed reporters unconstitutional.
CNN, Politico and MS NOW filed their lawsuit Monday arguing that the president’s move violated the defendants’ due process rights and First Amendment protections for newsgathering and speech.
The three outlets said they were filing the lawsuit “to protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes.”

U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, who was appointed by Trump in 2017, will preside over the hearing Wednesday. He will evaluate the outlets’ request to issue a temporary restraining order blocking enforcement of the ban and restoring reporters’ hard passes to access White House grounds.
Kelly ruled against Trump in a similar case back in 2018, when the White House withdrew credentials from reporter Jim Acosta, who was then with CNN.

On Tuesday, Trump remarked that he would “probably” ​let journalists from CNN, ⁠MS ​NOW and ​Politico back into the White ​House if ​a court rules ‌against ⁠his decision to ban the ​media ​outlets ⁠from the White ​House grounds.

Later that day, during his address to the United Nations’ General Assembly in New York, Trump told CNN reporter Kaitlan Collins: “You shouldn’t be here ... You said you weren’t going to cover me.” Collins responded that CNN never said it was not going to cover Trump, and that while it had been banned from the White House it was credentialed by the U.N. as usual.

The solidarity among TV networks has been swift, as they refused to provide TV pool coverage of the president’s activities this week, resulting in quiet mics and a lack of photographs of Trump’s official activities.

Pool coverage is when one network attends an event and then distributes information and media, such as video footage and audio, to other outlets. The system has been recognized by administrations from both parties for decades, and the coverage is used by pool members and subscribers, which includes outlets like Newsmax, One America News Network, C-SPAN and international outlets.

Print and radio pools are still in place, and TV pools for events for other parts of the administration will continue. Individual TV networks, including NBC News, continue to provide coverage of White House events that are open to the press, outside of the pool. Outside of events, NBC News reporters continue to report on the administration’s activities.

title: New campaign aims to help millions at risk of losing Medicaid coverage under work requirements
summary: On Jan. 1, new federal work and reporting requirements kick in for Medicaid, leaving millions at risk of losing healthcare coverage as states scramble to prepare for the most substantial change to the program in decades.
story: MECHANICSVILLE, Va. — In 100 days, on Jan. 1, new federal work and reporting requirements kick in for Medicaid recipients, leaving roughly 10 million Americans at risk of losing healthcare coverage, as states scramble to prepare for the most substantial change to the program in decades.

A new, $2 million campaign called “Keep Your Care,” an independent nonprofit, launched Wednesday. Shared exclusively with NBC News, it aims to educate states and Medicaid recipients ahead of the massive change.

For Melanie and Greg Stephens, who live in a small town outside of Richmond, Virginia, the resources can’t come soon enough. On Aug. 31, the family received a letter in the mail informing them of the new guidelines.
“When I received the letter about all the changes coming up, I had a panic attack because I was like, ‘Oh, my gosh, what does this mean?’” Melanie Stephens said.
New Medicaid work requirements could put caregivers at risk of losing coverage

As full-time caregivers for their disabled daughter, Rachel, they are exempt from the 80-hours-per-month work or community service requirement that will affect most eligible adults in the new year. But they will still need to prove they are exempt every six months.

“Our concern is not so much on our part because we are thorough,” Greg Stephens said. “Once it leaves us and goes to a Medicaid worker to process, that’s where we are concerned they’re going to miss a deadline or fall through the cracks, and we have no control over that.”

The work requirements, supported by Republicans to address wasteful spending, were passed as part of the “big, beautiful bill” signed into law by President Donald Trump last year. But they could leave eligible recipients without coverage because of the administrative hoops they will now have to jump through, health care advocates argue.
Virginia Health Secretary Marvin Figueroa, in an interview with NBC News, described it as “fighting government for something that you’re entitled to.”

“I go back to just look at the debate that allowed this bill to pass. This is a predictable surprise,” he added. “The discussion was about losing coverage, and I think we’re going to see that across the board.”

Senate Majority Leader John Thune and many Republicans defended the cuts at the time, arguing they were “targeting waste, fraud, and abuse in the program” and also “want to make sure that this doesn’t hurt beneficiaries.”

“And what’s being said out there by the Democrats is totally inaccurate,” Thune said in an interview last year, days before his chamber voted to pass the legislation. “It doesn’t cut Medicaid … What we’re talking about here is getting rid of waste, fraud and abuse, strengthening and improving the program for the people who need it the most and for whom it was intended, and really making this program more solvent for the long term.”

Keep Your Care was established by two health care advocacy groups, Caring Across Generations and the Healthcare Education Project, and the Service Employees International Union. The group’s state-level work will focus on Georgia, North Carolina, Illinois, Michigan, California, Virginia and New York, states with Medicaid expansion under the Affordable Care Act where millions stand to lose coverage. The group is working with communities to help eligible Americans maintain coverage, and influence state and local governments on how the new requirements are implemented. Its website will list state-specific information about what is changing, determine the requirements and exemptions that may apply and track reporting deadlines.

Greg Stephens admitted that, as a physician, he judged patients who were covered by Medicaid until he became a recipient himself. But his daughter Rachel, 22, has faced increasing health challenges since Covid and requires 24/7 management: so much so that he quit his job last year, just as his wife had years before. With no income on paper, they had to apply for Medicaid.

“We spent months calling other insurance companies and other agents and trying to find another way, and there was no other way,” Melanie Stephens shared during an interview at their home, accomplished because Rachel’s grandparents looked after her during the 30-minute window.

The coverage allows the Stephens to care for Rachel, who is bound to a wheelchair, at home, which also means administering medications five times per day and feeding her through a tube. Rachel’s care is so complex that the only other option for their daughter, the Stephens said, would be an institution.
“There’s no one that could possibly care for her medically, or emotionally or cognitively,” the Stephens shared, adding: “She would have no will to live.”

The Stephens acknowledged that while there may be some individuals on Medicaid who could work, the changes made were an overcorrection, burdening eligible families with unnecessary stress and paperwork.
“There’s a lot of people that are getting health care through Medicaid expansion, like ourselves, that absolutely need this exclusion to be able to do what we do,” Greg Stephens said.

title: Capt. Sully Sullenberger speaks out about Alzheimer’s diagnosis: ‘I’ve done harder things’
summary: For the first time since announcing his Alzheimer’s diagnosis over the summer, Capt. Sully Sullenberger discusses the impact on his life.
story: For the first time since announcing his Alzheimer’s diagnosis over the summer, Capt. Chesley “Sully” Sullenberger has discussed his experience with the disease and what lies ahead.

“I’ve done harder things than this before,” Sullenberger, the  retired pilot who successfully landed a commercial airliner filled with passengers on the Hudson River in 2009, told “Good Morning America” on Wednesday.
Sullenberger, 75, and his wife, Lorrie Sullenberger, spoke to host Robin Roberts about the diagnosis, which he revealed in a post on his website in July.

“I recently found out I have been diagnosed with Alzheimer’s Disease. It is early stage,” Sullenberger wrote in the July 14 post. “For now, this means a name may not come easily to me, I forget a story I have recently told, or I don’t sleep as well, but I am in the beginning of this long journey.”

Sullenberger became a household name when he successfully landed a commercial airplane in the Hudson River, saving everyone on board, after a bird strike caused both engines to fail shortly after takeoff. The act has since been known as “The Miracle on the Hudson.”
Clint Eastwood dramatized Sullenberger’s heroic exploits in the 2016 film “Sully,” starring Tom Hanks in the titular role.
Roberts on Wednesday asked Sullenberger to compare his diagnosis to that heroic moment.

“We had to devise a plan, execute that plan flawlessly for the first time — never having done it before — and save every life in 208 seconds,” Sullenberger recalled. He added, “had even one person not survived, I would have considered it a tragic failure.”

“So I think we’re we’re doing the same thing here,” he continued of his diagnosis. “We’re focusing clearly on the highest priority items first, and we are ignoring everything we don’t have time to do.”

Sullenberger is receiving monthly treatments for the disease, which aims to slow the condition. Both he and his wife said initially, they wanted to keep his diagnosis private, but later decided to speak out with the hope that they could help others.
“This is a disease, not a character flaw,” Lorrie Sullenberger said.  “I think we need to talk about it more openly, and maybe other people can do the same.”
Sullenberger added that at first, he questioned: “Why me?”
But, “we’re not by any means alone,” he reflected. “We’re part of this community who are trying to make the best of a bad situation.”
Sullenberger said the first signs of the disease were forgetting things that he normally wouldn’t, like people’s names — even those he has known for a long time — and events.
The symptoms were easy to dismiss in the beginning, his wife said, because they were so minor. She noted that what a lot of people see in the news are cases of late-stage Alzheimer’s disease.
“If you have doubts, get tested because the sooner you act, the more options there are, the better the outcome is likely to be,” Sullenberger said.
One of the couple’s daughters, Kelly Sullenberger, told Roberts that since her dad’s diagnosis, her priority has been spending more time with their family.
“Our family likes to be prepared and have plans in place. It runs in our blood, and it’s something that you can’t really plan for,” she said.
Sullenberger, who is set to be inducted into the National Aviation Hall of Fame this month, told Roberts that his greatest concern is “that this is my last flight.”
“But if this has to be my last flight,” he said, “I’m going to go out using full afterburner.”

title: Nolan Wells’ family vows to ‘never stop’ seeking the truth after grand jury report
summary: Nolan Wells’ parents and their attorneys called on Mississippi to continue pursuing a fuller picture of the “truth” in the teenager’s death at a news conference Tuesday.
story: Nolan Wells’ parents and their attorneys called on Mississippi to continue pursuing a fuller picture of the “truth” in the teenager’s death at a news conference Tuesday.
The news conference was held a day after the Jackson County district attorney said a state grand jury will not pursue charges in the teenager’s July Fourth death.

“Jackson County District Attorney Angel Myers McArthur will have you accept that Nolan Wells’ death can be summarized in three words: ‘We’ll never know,’” attorney Ben Crump said. “But Nolan’s family offers three other words: ‘We’ll never stop.’”
Crump, in his remarks, insinuated that the district attorney’s investigation was not exhaustive and should continue until the cause of Wells’ death is made clear.
Add to Google
Add to Google
Wells’ mother, Christine Wells-Wonsley, said she received a text message from the district attorney at 7:54 p.m. Monday, and that the report was released shortly after.
“To me, that action shows a lack of empathy,” she said.
Wells-Wonsley continued: “What we have learned is that we still have no answers, and the report reinforced the fact that Nolan was not given a thorough, transparent and honest investigation.”

The DA’s office shared the text with NBC News. It alerts Wells-Wonsley to the grand jury report, without revealing its conclusions. The DA offers to send it to Wells-Wonsley and offers to “support you in your grief.”

Wells, 18, was last seen celebrating the July 4 holiday with friends on Horn Island, a barrier reef off Mississippi accessible only by boat. The friends he was with that day have said they had to leave the island early because their boat was taking on water, and that Wells opted to stay behind for the rest of the day and told them he’d catch a ride back to the mainland with others.
His body was found at the northwestern tip of the island July 6, Crump has said.

In the aftermath of Wells’ death, Crump pointed the blame toward the friends Wells was with on that day, all of whom are white, and alleged that race played a role. Wells appeared to be one of the few Black people on the island that day, according to photos and videos shared of the celebrations.
District Attorney Angel Myers McIlrath attempted to put that idea to rest with Tuesday’s statement.
In a video message, she said the grand jury did not find sufficient evidence to indict anyone with a crime.

“There is absolutely no evidence to support the allegations that Nolan’s disappearance and death were racially motivated,” Myers McIlrath said. “Nolan’s friends loved Nolan, and Nolan loved them. Nolan chose to stay on the island that day, and there is not a scintilla of evidence to contradict that.”

In an interview with NBC News, Wells-Wonsley said that “at no point in time have we ever made this a racial thing” but that “Unfortunately, the optics of the situation has kind of allowed a segue to that.”
She said that she and her husband, Elmore Wonsley, have only wanted to find out what happened to their son.
“I have always told our children, ‘I will move heaven and earth if anything were to ever happen,’ and that’s exactly what Elmore and I are doing,” she said.
Myers McIlrath took aim at Crump and his team on Monday, saying they’d previously informed her office that they’d found no evidence a crime had been committed against Wells.
Speaking with NBC News on Tuesday, Crump said he did not want to engage in a “tit for tat” with the DA and her office.
“The issue is about what happened to Nolan Wells,” he said. “Everything else is just a distraction.”
The Rev. Al Sharpton, who has been an advocate for the family, said skepticism is warranted from Wells’ parents and those following the case.

“Mississippi’s history painfully teaches us exactly why families should never be expected to simply accept unanswered questions surrounding the death of a young Black person,” the civil rights advocate said in a statement Tuesday.
Crump, along with Wells’ parents, commissioned an independent autopsy, which found the cause of the teenager’s death was “undetermined.” It did, however, find two bruises on the back of Wells’ head.

“To this day, not one person has explained how they got there,” Crump said in a statement. “We don’t know how Nolan died, and neither does the state of Mississippi. Mississippi must keep investigating.”
Crump and Wells-Wonsley both spoke about the apparent blunt force trauma again Tuesday at the news conference and called for answers.

The grand jury’s report, a partially redacted copy of of which was posted to the DA’s Facebook page, noted the bruising to the back of Wells’ head but concluded that it was “not a fatal injury.” A witness, it said, testified to seeing Wells awkwardly off the boat. The witness couldn’t tell if Wells hit his head but said he continued to socialize, the report stated.
Crump also called on the district attorney to release the full autopsy report from the medical examiner’s office.

Coroner Bruce Lynd said he will not be releasing the state’s autopsy report, telling NBC News the report, “which may include a toxicology report, cannot be released because the release of autopsy reports” is limited by Mississippi law.

The grand jury concluded that there was no evidence that Wells had any sort of physical altercation or argument with anyone the day he was last seen. It added “that the position of, the condition of, time of discovery, and location of Mr. Wells’ body is consistent with drowning.”

Crump and Wells’ parents have previously rejected the idea that he simply drowned, citing the teenager’s athleticism and ability to swim. Those who know the area well, though, told NBC News it is not uncommon for even a good swimmer to be swept away by the currents.

The state’s chief medical examiner and a forensic pathologist retained by Wells’ family both “opined that the cause and manner of Mr. Wells’ death is undetermined and that drowning is a diagnosis of exclusion,” according to the grand jury report. It noted, however, that neither has ruled out accidental drowning as a cause.

Crump said there will be another press conference in Orlando, Florida, later this week to discuss the investigation into Wells’ cellphone. The friends on the boat had his phone and brought it back to the mainland from Horn Island on July 4. They said Wells accidentally left it with them, but his parents have refuted that assertion, asking what teenager would leave their phone behind?

title: Jon Hamm Opens Up About Becoming a Dad on TODAY, Including the 1 Thing He’s Most Excited About
summary: Jon Hamm and wife Anna Osceola are expecting their first child. The “Your Friends & Neighbors” co-stars married in June 2023.
story: Jon Hamm and wife Anna Osceola now have one additional outfit for their little one.

The former “Mad Men” star appeared on TODAY Sept. 23 to talk about his new series “American Hostage” on MGM+ in which he plays a radio host thrust into a crisis in 1977 when a hostage-taker  demands he take his call on air.
During his chat with Craig Melvin, Hamm also spoke about expecting his first child with Osceola.

“It’s great,” Hamm said. “The best thing I keep hearing is how much it changes you for the better. I’m very excited. I’ve been around kids my whole life. I’ve been a teacher, my nieces and nephews and all that stuff, so I’m excited to start our own family.
“And it’s thrilling. And terrifying.”
The couple are gathering all the essentials that their newborn will need, including plenty of onesies.
Now, they’ll have one more, as the anchors surprised Hamm with a special TODAY onesie in honor of Hamm’s professed love for Bravo programming and “The Real Housewives” franchise.
The special onesie reads, “Going to bed, so daddy can watch Bravo.”
“Beautiful,” Hamm said. “This will get used, I can tell you that much.”
Hamm also received a special message from Sonja Morgan, a former cast member of “The Real Housewives of New York City.”
The “Your Friends & Neighbors” co-stars were first rumored to be welcoming a child in August.
Hamm, 55, and Osceola, 38, tied the knot in June 2023.
The following year, Hamm opened up to The Hollywood Reporter about possibly starting a family with his new bride.
Hamm told the publication his parents’ divorce when he was young initially turned him off of the idea of marriage. But all that changed when he met Osceola.

“Obviously, my parents were not married long,” said Hamm, whose mom died when he was 10, “so I don’t have a model to look at and go, ‘Oh, this is how one finds happiness.’ I just knew at a certain point I wanted to be with this person. But when I proposed, I was terrified. I was like, ‘What am I doing?’”
The actor went on to say he and Osceola enjoyed a “perfect” wedding day in Big Sur at the same location the “Mad Men” finale was filmed nine years before.
The “emotional” event, he said, gave him “a reset, a reboot, a reframe, a reimagining.”
“So, it’s been great. And I hope it turns into kids. It’s not lost on me that I’m 53. I will be the old dad, but so it goes. It could be a good thing. We’ll see,” Hamm said.
Less than a year before getting hitched, Hamm opened up about his relationship with Osceola during a September 2022 interview on Howard Stern’s SiriusXM show.

“This is another place in my life that I feel very settled and comfortable. I’m in a relationship right now and ... it’s comfortable,” he said, adding, “It’s about taking care of someone else and being taken care of.”

Hamm revealed that after undergoing therapy to work on the “wound” of losing his mother at such a young age, he had become “opened up the possibility of things like being married, having kids, defining a new version of happiness, life, wellness.”
“It sounds hokey and whatever, but it’s real and for want of a better word, it’s what I’m working for. What else is there other than that?”

title: Ina Garten Recalls the First Employee She Ever Fired — and the Hilarious Way It Backfired
summary: On an episode of Making Space, Hoda Kotb asks Ina Garten how she is successful while remaining kind. She shares a funny story that taught her a lesson about clarity.
story: When Ina Garten bought a small specialty food store called Barefoot Contessa on a whim, she knew nothing about running a business. Over the decades that followed, she built the store — and herself — into a household name, with bestselling cookbooks, hit Food Network shows and, most recently, a new podcast, “Happy Hour with Ina Garten.”
Garten is clearly a powerful, decisive businesswoman, but her public persona is one built on connection and warmth.

When the 78-year old sat down with Hoda Kotb for the September 23 episode of the “Making Space” podcast, Kotb points out that Garten has built an enormously successful career without appearing to “swing some sharp elbows” along the way. So how, she wondered, do you get to the top while remaining “sweet and kind”?
I think the two sides of me that seem diametrically opposed, which they’re really not, is kindness and clarity.
Ina Garten

“I think the two sides of me that seem diametrically opposed, which they’re really not, is kindness and generosity and warmth, but also clarity,” Garten replies. “Clarity can look tough, because I know what I want, and that’s what I want. And it doesn’t have to be mean.”
Garten says it was a lesson from her therapist, during her early days running Barefoot Contessa, that taught her how to strike that balance.

“I was running the store, and I was beside myself. I was just too exhausted. And [my therapist] said, ‘Your employees need two things from you: They need you to be clear and they need you to be happy.’”
But Garten admits clarity didn’t always come naturally to her — particularly when she first became a boss.

“I had to learn that.” she says. “The first person I fired was this sweet young woman. Oh my God, she was so sweet, and it was the first summer, and she was just terrible. And I took her out in the back, and I said, you know, maybe this isn’t the job for you, but maybe another job would be.”
Garten delivered the bad news so gently that her employee didn’t realize she’d been fired.

“The next day she showed up for work. I was so gentle; she didn’t know she was fired!” she recalls. “I let her stay for the rest of the summer because I couldn’t do it again. I already did it one time. I was so afraid I broke her spirit.”
Eventually, Garten learned that being kind and being clear aren’t opposites.
“If somebody’s not happy and not doing a good job, they know it. I would just convince them this isn’t the right job for them. But maybe [something else] would be a great job for them.”
Garten recalls sharing an office with her accountant at the time, who was often surprised by how employees reacted after Garten let them go.
“I would fire them, and then they would leave, and she’d go, ‘How did you do that? They thanked you when they left. What did you just say?’”
Her secret?
“We’re clear. We’re not tough. We’re clear,” she says.
