title: What Dolly Parton Was Like ‘On a Personal Note,’  According to Kelly Clarkson
summary: Kelly Clarkson will always have a special place in her heart for Dolly Parton.
story: Kelly Clarkson will always have a special place in her heart for Dolly Parton.
Following the country legend’s death on Aug. 25, Clarkson opened up about her relationship with Parton while stopping by Studio 1A Sept. 21.
“She was just very cool as a human, not only as a musician,” she said.
Clarkson called Parton “such a lovely woman” and said she was “very sweet” and “very cool.”
“Even the first time I met her, (it) was like we’ve known each other for years,” she said.
Clarkson, who recently wrapped up her final season of “The Kelly Clarkson Show,” selected one of Parton’s most famous songs, “9 to 5,” to open the first episode of her talk show in 2019.
“That was our first cover. That was the first Kellyoke,” she recalled.
Clarkson described Parton as a “beautiful soul” and said she was a “pioneer for a lot of women.”
“She just paved the way for so many,” she said. “But on a personal note, she was so nice every time we ran into each other, like she was just so cool.”
In 2022, Clarkson had the opportunity to honor Parton during the ACM Awards and perform a rendition of the country crooner’s hit song, “I Will Always Love You.
While appearing on TODAY, Clarkson recalled how she felt when she was asked to pay tribute to Parton.

“I was like, ‘Of course! I’ll show up. Where do you want me?’ And then they were like, ‘Oh, she picked this song.’ And I was like, ‘What?’ I was like, ‘You want me to sing which one?’ And I was very nervous because that’s not a song anyone wants to touch. But yeah, but I would for her,” she said.
The same year, Parton and Clarkson teamed up for a duet of “9 to 5” for the documentary “Still Working 9 to 5.” At the time, Parton applauded Clarkson for her fresh take on the famous song.
“Nobody sings like Kelly Clarkson. She makes any song come alive,” Parton said in a press release, per People. “I love her voice on ‘9 to 5,’ and I am so proud I got to sing with her on it.”

title: ‘The Voice’ Welcomes 2 New Coaches for Milestone Season 30
summary: “The Voice” Season 30 has two new coaches sitting in the famous red chairs. Find out who is joining reigning champ Adam Levine and Kelly Clarkson.
story: “The Voice” will soon usher in the reign of a new queen for its milestone Season 30, and possibly an artist who is looking to take Blake Shelton’s king of country crown.

As the new season of “The Voice” kicks off, here are the official four coaches who are seated in the spinning red chairs when the singing competition series premieres. Joining returning coaches Adam Levine and Kelly Clarkson are two newcomers: country music singer Riley Green and icon Queen Latifah.
Levine was the first coach to be announced for Season 30 as “The Voice” officially announced “the champion” would be back in April. Then, Clarkson was confirmed on May 7.
“The Voice” waited a few days before surprising fans with the special announcement that two new faces were joining the NBC family.
Riley Green Takes a Seat in the Red Chair
On May 10, the show posted an Instagram video of Green, a four-time CMA and four-time ACM winner, listening to a voice message from Clarkson in which she welcomed him to the crew.

In the clip, she greeted him and said, “I’m super stoked to work alongside you. Welcome to ‘The Voice.’ I was stoked when I heard you were going to be a coach because I’m actually a super-fan of your music, man. You’re so good.”

She then added, “Needless to say, it is a competition so I, as a future friend, sent you something.” Clarkson explained that the gift was meant to help him prepare for his time as a coach before she “whooped that a--.”
“The Voice” later uploaded a video of Green sitting in his chair and practicing pressing his red button.
Queen Latifah Is Ready to Reign
The show saved Queen Latifah’s grand reveal for last, confirming her debut in a press release May 12.
Queen Latifah, already a Grammy, Emmy and Golden Globe winner with an Academy Award nomination, will soon try to add a “Voice” championship to her long list of accolades.

The multi-hyphenate and Green will look to dethrone Team Adam, who secured a victory in the Season 29 “Battle of Champions” finale in April with Alexia Jayy taking home the trophy. Levine and Clarkson are now tied with four wins each behind original coach Shelton, who won nine times.
Season 30 of “The Voice” premieres with a three-night premiere event starting Monday, Sept. 21 at 8 p.m.

title: Taylor Swift’s 3-Word Reaction to Travis Kelce’s 1st Touchdown of the Football Season
summary: Taylor Swift had an adorable show of support for her husband Travis Kelce after his first touchdown of the Chiefs 2026 season.
story: Taylor Swift’s show of support for Travis Kelce at the latest Kansas City Chiefs game left onlookers swooning.
The “Opalite” singer was spotted cheering on her husband at Arrowhead Stadium Sept. 20 during their game against the Indianapolis Colts.
Sporting a Chiefs tank top and jeans, the newlywed couldn’t contain her excitement as Kelce scored his first touchdown of the 2026 season.
As other fans in the stands began to cheer, Swift proudly pointed at her engagement ring and wedding band and said, “That’s my husband!” Then she proceeded to clap for the Chiefs tight end.
The NFL and Chiefs Instagram pages captured the moment and shared it, captioning the post, “@taylorswift is a proud wife after @killatrav’s TD ❤️.”
Fans of the couple, who tied the knot at Madison Square Garden in July, took to the comments section to share their love for Swift’s show of affection for her husband.
“Good job Travis, love how proud she is😍😍😍,” one commented.
“Love this couple! Pure joy,” another wrote.
One fan weighed in, writing, “I love this ❤️🙌🔥👏 Taylor is so excited for her husband and his team. I absolutely adore her. Never stop being you, Taylor. Your laughter and joy are infectious.”
Swift is jubilant in the stands, but has received criticism for the attention she’s given at games. The NFL regularly pans the camera to the singer during games.

In a 2023 interview with Time, Swift addressed the topic, saying, “I’m just there to support Travis,” she said. “I have no awareness of if I’m being shown too much and p------ off a few dads, Brads, and Chads.”
Referencing the quote, one Swiftie shared the following reaction to the latest video of the singer supporting Kelce: “It’s going to be a long football season for the ‘Dads, Brad’s and Chad’s hahaha.”
The 2026 football season only recently kicked off. On Sept. 14, Swift attended the Chiefs season opener and sat next to Tom Cruise.
While appearing on “The Tonight Show,” the actor later told Jimmy Fallon about the conversation he had with the singer.
“She was schooling me on football,” he said.
Cruise called the singer “a genius” and said he’s been “following her since she was a kid.”
“She’s funny. She’s got such a great sense of humor,” he said.

title: Gwyneth Paltrow Reveals Story Behind Her ‘Conscious Uncoupling’ With Chris Martin
summary: When Gwyneth Paltrow and Chris Martin used the term “conscious uncoupling” to describe their separation in 2014, the phrase ended up going viral at the time, taking the internet by storm.
story: When Gwyneth Paltrow and Chris Martin used the term “conscious uncoupling” to describe their separation in 2014, the phrase ended up going viral at the time, taking the internet by storm.
And now, we finally have its backstory.

Paltrow, 53, opened up about the term during a recent episode of podcast “Friends Keep Secrets.” It turns out, her introduction to the phrase came from a therapist that she and Martin had at the time.

“Chris and I had this therapist that was really brilliant, and he sort of introduced us to the concept,” Paltrow told hosts Benny Blanco, Lil Dicky and his wife Kristin Batalucco during the Sept. 8 episode. “We just made a commitment to really put the kids first, and so what that meant was to stay a family, even though we weren’t a couple.”
Paltrow — who is currently married to writer and director Brad Falchuk, 55 — shares two children with Martin, 49. The two announced the news of the divorce through a statement on her Goop website.

“We are parents first and foremost, to two incredibly wonderful children and we ask for their and our space and privacy to be respected at this difficult time,” Paltrow and Martin wrote in the statement. “We have always conducted our relationship privately, and we hope that as we consciously uncouple and coparent, we will be able to continue in the same manner.”
Paltrow told the podcast that when she and Martin decided to get divorced, she turned to friends who came from divorced households for guidance.

“I said, ‘Tell me, what was the worst thing? What do you feel you have scars from to this day?’” Paltrow recounted. “They said the worst part was ... ‘My dad used to drop me off at the end of the driveway.’ ‘It was so tense at my birthday parties.’ ‘They never ate dinner in the same room until my college graduation, and it caused me so much pain.’”

She added that she and Martin sought to “circumvent all of that awful stuff.” Paltrow also shared one particular trying moment during the divorce in which she had to put the conscious uncoupling philosophy to work. She explained that when the family moved to Los Angeles early on in the separation, they continued to have brunch together every Sunday. One particular brunch date proved difficult.

“Chris and I were upset with each other about something – I can’t even remember what it is — and I was like, ‘This might go really off the rails,’” she recalled. “It was getting tense, and we looked at each other. We went outside on the front porch, and we’re like, ‘Let’s just not.’”
She said that the two ended up embracing.
“We just hugged,” she said. “We like fist-bumped and then we went to brunch.”

Paltrow, to be clear, did not invent the term “conscious uncoupling.” The tactic, believed to be coined by late marriage and family therapist Katherine Woodward Thomas, has long existed with therapists and counselors encouraging the mindset as part of the final stage of marriage counseling after a decision to divorce is made.
Life coach Jeanne Byrd Romero previously told TODAY.com that conscious uncoupling is a method that can help the parties heal.
“It’s really a way of moving out of blame and shame so people can transform the experience into healing and peace,” Romero said. “It can be done with just one of the partners are the couple.”

title: Miley Cyrus Shares Her One Hilarious, Relatable Fear About Getting Married To Maxx Morando
summary: Singer Miley Cyrus recently shared the one reservation she has about getting married to fiancé Maxx Morando — and it is oh, so relatable.
story: Singer Miley Cyrus recently shared the one reservation she has about getting married to fiancé Maxx Morando — and it is oh, so relatable.
Cyrus, 33, spoke about the relationship in a Sept. 17 interview with Apple Music’s Zane Lowe. The singer, who got engaged to Morando last year, was brutally honest about her fears.

“We’ve been together six years, and I’ve never gotten the ick. But I was like, all of a sudden, got in my head,” Cyrus told Lowe. “I was like, ‘Oh my god, I’m about to get married. What if I get the ick?’”
The ick, of course, refers to that sudden onset of feeling of disgust when a love interest does something one finds awkward, embarrassing or gross.
Morando pretty successfully squashed the fear, Cyrus said.

“I asked him, ‘What happens if you get the ick once you’re married?’ He’s like, ‘You deal with it, and like you move on, and you don’t be a baby. The ick is for when you’re in fifth grade,’” she said.

Cyrus, who got engaged to Morando in Kyoto, Japan, has previously been married once to actor Liam Hemsworth. The pair separated in 2019 after eight months of marriage. The “Flowers” singer then met Morando on a blind date years later in 2021.
In the interview with Lowe, Cyrus said that her experience with the ick was put to the test shortly after she talked the subject with Morando.
“Then suddenly I got the ick,” Cyrus shared. “He did something that icked me for a minute, and I was like, ‘Don’t ever do that again. It gave me the ick.’”
It led her to wonder if she’s ever given her partner the ick as well, Cyrus told Lowe.
“He said, ‘When you’re a brat,’” Cyrus said of Morando’s ick. “Which is so true. Dude, I’m so icky when I’m a brat.”

Cyrus and Morando have been rather private about their relationship, sparingly attending events together. However both have spoken highly of one another. In a July interview with Wonderland Magazine, Morando said that he loves “going with her to certain things to support whatever she’s doing.”
Cyrus told Lowe in their chat that Morando has allowed her to “soften.”
“I realized so much of my life was performative that I didn’t even realize that he’s given me the permission to really like soften into the reality,” she said.

The pair have also collaborated professionally, with Morando co-writing multiple songs with Cyrus. Recently, the couple appeared together in the steamy music video for her aptly-titled song “Let’s Get Married,” shot at the Chateau Marmont in Los Angeles. The song is part of her new album “Bass Persuades,” which debuted on Sept. 18.

title: Alexis Ohanian Shares 1 Sweet Rule He And Serena Williams Have For Their Daughters
summary: Reddit co-founder Alexis Ohanian shared how he and his wife, tennis icon Serena Williams approach their kids’ aspirations in life.
story: Reddit co-founder Alexis Ohanian shared how he and his wife, tennis icon Serena Williams approach their kids’ aspirations in life.

Ohanian — who spoke to reporters Sept. 18 at the international debut of his all-women track and field league, Athlos, in London — told USA Sports that the couple just has one rule when it comes to the future careers of young daughters Olympia, 9, and Adira, 3.
“The one rule in the house is we don’t care what you want to do when you grow up, as long as you do your best at it and you’re doing something useful,” Ohanian, 43, told the outlet.

Ohanian attended the event with Williams, 44, along with their two children in a rare family appearance all together. The meet also included Olympic gold medalist sprinters Sha’Carri Richardson and Gabby Thomas, who are also two of the league’s athlete-owner advisors.
Ohanian explained to USA Sports that that day, Williams was tasked with monitoring their youngest, Adira. Meanwhile, Olympia was out, interviewing the star athletes.
Ohanian explained to the outlet that while Olympia was comfortable chatting it up with the athletes, she’s not firm on becoming a journalist.
“She hasn’t mentioned journalist yet,” Ohanian told the outlet. Right now, fashion designer is the number one career path that she’s circling around.”
He joked to the outlet’s journalist that their job is “safe for now, but watch out.”
“She’s coming for journalism,” he said. “She’s gonna go be great.”
Ohanian and Williams welcomed Olympia in September 2017 while Adira was born in August 2023. They’ve previously spoken about honoring their kids’ own passions.

In a January interview with TODAY hosts Jenna Bush Hager and Sheinelle Jones, Williams shared that her children are in different sports that align with their personalities. Olympia, for example, is more interested in golf because she doesn’t like to run, Williams said, laughing. Adira may end up being the tennis player in the family, she added.

title: Celine Dion Dances Barefoot Atop Car After Paris Show In Ultimate Display Of Queen Behavior
summary: After a Sept. 18 show at the Plenitude Arena just outside Paris, France, power ballad icon Celine Dion surprised fans outside of her hotel with an impromptu performance in which she climbed up on the roof of a car barefoot and sang along with the giant crowd.
story: The queen is in her element.

After a Sept. 18 show at the Plenitude Arena just outside Paris, France, power ballad icon Celine Dion surprised fans outside of her hotel with an impromptu performance in which she climbed up on the roof of a car barefoot and sang along with the giant crowd.

Her iconic fan interaction comes amid her ongoing Paris residency that marks her first concerts in six years. Dion previously took a break from the stage after publicly revealing her stiff person syndrome diagnosis.
Multiple fan videos captured the magical moment. And it’s clear that the “My Heart Will Go On” singer is soaking it all up.

In the videos, Dion is seen climbing on top of the car and clapping along to her song “Pour que tu m’aimes encore.” Dressed in a more casual jacket and baggy pants, Dion engages with the enthusiastic crowd, dancing, playing air guitar and more.   She’s loving every second.

The past few weeks have been particularly significant for the artist, who has been performing in the City of Love amid a 26-date residency. During her first show back on Sept. 12, Dion made an emotional speech, reflecting on her return.
“I had promised myself not to cry,” said Dion, breaking down in tears. “But I’m so happy to see you all. I missed you.”
She added that she had always promised to come back to the stage — a commitment she kept.

“So here I am, singing for you,” Dion said during that first show at Plenitude Arena. “Thank you so very much for your support, your patience and if I may say so, I am everything I am because you loved me.”
Dion told the world about her diagnosis in 2022, canceling a string of performances at the time to navigate the condition.

Stiff person syndrome, a progressive, neurological disorder, causes stiff muscles in the torso, arms and legs, according to the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke. People with the syndrome can also experience greater sensitivity to noise, touch and emotional distress which can set off muscle spasms.
In the September cover story of Harper’s Bazaar, Dion revealed that she had experienced symptoms of the condition for 17 years prior to her diagnosis.

title: Ruby Rose Tears Up, Remembering Friend Hayden Panettiere: ‘We Spoke Every Day For 5 Years’
summary: Actor Ruby Rose recently got emotional while reflecting on the bond she shared with her good friend and confidante Hayden Panettiere, who died in August.
story: Actor Ruby Rose recently got emotional while reflecting on the bond she shared with her good friend and confidante Hayden Panettiere, who died in August.

Rose spoke about Panettiere’s passing during a Sept. 18 interview with Entertainment Tonight, sharing details about the friendship that the two shared over the years. The comments come weeks after Panettiere was found unresponsive at an apartment in Greenville, South Carolina. She was 36.

Rose — who was promoting the upcoming season of reality show “Special Forces: World’s Toughest Test,” on which she is a cast member — began to tear up while speaking about her connection with the late actor.
“That was my best friend,” Rose told the outlet. “We spoke every day for five years.”
Speaking to the outlet ahead of the show’s premiere on Sept. 24, Rose, 40, also revealed the way in which she met Panettiere.
“I didn’t even think we were going to be friends,” Rose said. “I didn’t know if I wanted to have any celebrity friends because I ... don’t have a great experience with the industry.”
Rose explained that while she was initially hesitant to befriend Panettiere, her reservations quickly dissolved.

“She saw me, and I just remember thinking, ‘Oh no!’ And then she ran up anyway and was like, ‘Hey, I’m Hayden. Can we go talk somewhere? We’ve got a lot in common,’” Rose said. “And then we went and talked, and we had everything in common.”
Rose told Entertainment Tonight that she and Panettiere would chat daily, texting and “checking in on each another.”
“It’s a bigger group now. There’s 14 of us that we’ve collected over the years,” Rose said. “That’s really — that’s my family.”
Rose added that all Panettiere “really ever wanted was to have her story told — her way on her terms.”
Panettiere was in cardiac arrest, meaning her heart had stopped beating, when emergency personnel arrived to the apartment on Aug. 16. Her cause of death has not yet been released.

Chief Deputy Coroner Shelton England of the Greenville County, South Carolina Coroner’s Office told NBC News Sept. 16 that the final toxicology results — that will determine Panettiere’s official cause and manner of death — are expected to be released within the next two weeks, he estimated, or possibly sooner.

Both Panettiere and Rose have been vocal about their negative experiences in the entertainment industry. Panettiere reflected on the trauma she endured first as a child actor and later on as an adult in Hollywood in her memoir, “This Is Me: A Reckoning,” published in May 2026.
“Reality merged with my imagination and burrowed into my core memories, where all my shame and trauma lived. Is it any wonder why I’ve faced so many real struggles in my life?” she wrote.

Rose has also voiced many of her difficult experiences. In 2021, she alleged that she was fired from the CW’s “Batwoman” after she was seriously injured on set. Warner Bros. Television Group denied the allegations, saying in a statement Rose was fired over multiple complaints about her behavior.
Since Panettiere’s death, Rose has posted on social media about the painful loss.
“Missing Hayden more than life today,” Rose wrote in a Sept. 14 Threads post.

title: Trump tells U.N. he could ‘annihilate’ Iran but expects a deal after the midterm elections
summary: In a speech to world leaders at the United Nations General Assembly, President Donald Trump defended the Iran conflict and said he was considering whether to “annihilate” the country and drive it “into hell.”
story: In a speech to world leaders at the United Nations General Assembly, President Donald Trump defended the Iran conflict and said he was considering whether to “annihilate” the country and drive it “into hell.”
Or, he said, Iran could make a deal with the U.S. that would allow the nation to rebuild. But that won’t happen until after the midterm elections in November, Trump predicted.
“I believe we’ll make a deal right after the election because it doesn’t make sense for them not to,” Trump said. “They’re waiting to see how I do in the midterm election.”
Trump later said U.S. envoys met with Iranian officials for three hours on the sidelines of the gathering, an unexpected development that offered a glimpse of diplomatic activity.

But Trump has repeatedly floated new attacks on Iran, even previously threatening death to the entire civilization. On Tuesday, he revived that warning at one of the most prominent platforms for world leaders, with an Iranian delegation in the audience.

“I have a big decision to make,” he said. “Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before, maybe one of the greatest in the Middle East or even the world? Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again?”
“Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?” he continued.
Most important, Trump said to applause, is ensuring that “Iran will never have a nuclear weapon.”

Iran’s nuclear potential was “the reality we had to confront,” he argued, and “a reality that far too many preferred to ignore.” Tehran has insisted its nuclear program is for civilian purposes and denied having plans to develop nuclear weapons.
The U.N. assembly comes as the Iran war is about to enter its eighth month.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian is scheduled to address the U.N. on Wednesday. Trump told Fox News that he would “probably” be open to meeting with Pezeshkian but did not announce any specifics.
Add to Google
Add to Google
Trump also highlighted peace deals he has worked on, U.S. actions in the Western Hemisphere and progress on his 20-point peace plan in the Gaza Strip.

Trump’s remarks to the assembly this year come as the U.N.’s Human Rights Council found in a report last week “reasonable grounds to believe” that the U.S. had committed war crimes during “indiscriminate attacks” against an Iranian school and a residential area in February.
The American president traditionally addresses the General Assembly each year.
During his wide-ranging speech, the president said America is “doing better than ever before,” touting the U.S. economy and his approach to immigration and artificial intelligence.
America is ‘leading’
Less than a minute into his remarks, Trump called the U.S. economy “the envy of the world” and pointed to his administration’s tax policy and stock market records.
“Our economy is the envy of the world,” he said. “Our military is the most powerful on Earth. Our technology is second to none, and we are leading in virtually everything.”

Many American voters, though, don’t appear to agree. An NBC News poll conducted in September found that 56% of registered voters disapprove of the job the president is doing, and 55% said they believe his policies hurt the economy.

Gas prices remain high, sitting at an average of $4.47 per gallon, about a 50% increase since the war with Iran began. Diesel prices also spiked, affected by the Iran war as well as the war between Russia and Ukraine. Diesel hit a record $6 per gallon earlier this month before surging higher to $6.52 as of Tuesday, according to AAA.
Later, the president touted his record on immigration, tying his crackdown on the southern border to a drop in violent crime in the U.S.
“The entire world is being lifted by the wealth, strength, spirit and momentum of a newly energized and a very powerful United States of America,” he said.
Plans to ‘encourage’ AI
While Trump declined to endorse guardrails on artificial intelligence, he did push for one change: its name.

Trump said the U.S. would refer in official documents to “superintelligence,” rather than “artificial intelligence.” The word “artificial,” Trump argued, “makes it sound fake, and it is not fake. It’s actually amazing.”
Earlier this month, industry insiders warned that artificial intelligence could lead to human extinction, potentially in the next decade.
Trump said Tuesday that he would not “stifle growth of something that will be bigger than the Industrial Revolution.”
“We’re going to encourage it, not rein it in,” he said. “We’re going to watch it closely through the Department of Justice.”
Trump has previously said that the only guardrail the U.S. needs is “a STRONG AND SMART” president.
Artificial intelligence is also expected to be a main topic of conversation during Trump’s meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping this week.

Add to Google
Greenland, Ukraine and Venezuela

Trump met with several world leaders on the sidelines of the U.N. gathering, including Venezuela’s interim president, Delcy Rodríguez. It was Rodríguez’s first meeting with Trump since the U.S. captured then-Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, who are in a Brooklyn, New York, jail, awaiting trial.
Weeks ago, Trump said that the U.S. entered an agreement with Venezuela for U.S. majority control of more than 65 billion barrels of oil reserves in Venezuela.
On Tuesday, Trump called it “perhaps the biggest deal ever made,” adding: “To the victor belong the spoils.”

Trump said the Venezuela raid was “proof that the United States will no longer permit threats to America to gain a foothold anywhere in the Western Hemisphere,” noting U.S. attacks on drug cartels before pivoting to Cuba.
“My administration is seeking a fundamental change in the situation in Cuba,” he said, adding, “It will fall.”
In response, the Cuban delegation stood up and left the assembly hall.

Later Tuesday, Trump met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who said: “I hope that we will end this war, and President Trump will help us help us end this war,” Zelenskyy said.
Trump said during his speech that the war in Ukraine would end “more quickly than people understand.”
For years, the president said he would end the war. During his 2024 presidential campaign, he said he could end the war within 24 hours or even before his presidency began.
Last week, Trump signed into law a Russian sanctions bill championed by the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C.

He also announced that the U.S. would take over military operations and have “permanent control over security” in Greenland, in a deal signed later Tuesday with the leaders of Greenland and Denmark to try to end the tense standoff over the strategic Arctic territory.

title: The U.S. economy before and after the Iran war, in five charts
summary: On Feb. 27, the day before the United States and Israel attacked Iran, the American economy was on a steady course to lower inflation and attain greater buying power.
story: On Feb. 27, the day before the United States and Israel attacked Iran, the American economy was on a steady course to lower inflation and attain greater buying power. Gas was cheap and interest rates were coming down.
Today, none of those things are true anymore. When it comes to the U.S. economy, there’s before the Iran war — and since.

Despite assurances from President Donald Trump as early as March that the war would prove a “short-term excursion,” the conflict is about to round its seventh month. On Tuesday, Trump suggested that a deal could arrive after November’s midterm elections.

The morass has short-circuited Trump’s ability to tout other, more positive economic developments during his second term. The Census Bureau reported last week that the median U.S. household income hit an all-time high in 2025, while the percentage of people in the U.S. living in poverty fell to its lowest level on record. The stock market has done well this year, and the unemployment rate remains low.

Yet, on balance, the negative news has served to obscure the good, both for individual consumers and the nation at large. Before the war, gas prices were just under $3 a gallon. Today they’re at approximately $4.50 on average. Diesel prices went from an average of $3.75 on Feb. 28 to an all-time high of more than $6.50 on Tuesday.
This has caused a domino effect in which inflation rose, then borrowing costs, then mortgage rates.

Surveys of consumer sentiment and presidential approval polls continue to drift lower even as household spending on extras such as travel and dining out remains steady. In March, 35% of respondents to an NBC News poll said Trump had helped the economy. By September, that figure had declined to just 26%.
The White House defended the president’s record in a statement to NBC News.

“President Trump has always been clear about temporary disruptions as a result of the Iran conflict, but the Trump administration has remained laser-focused delivering on the President’s long-term economic agenda on the home front,” White House spokesman Kush Desai said in a statement.

The changes wrought by the war are nevertheless unmistakable. With less than six weeks until the midterm elections, the charts below offer the clearest picture yet of the challenge the White House faces as it works to retain Republican control of Congress.
Gas and diesel prices

The major reason for inflation’s run-up has been higher energy prices, especially fuel. Prior to the war’s launch, average gas prices stood at just under $3 a gallon, while diesel prices were less than $4 a gallon. Today, gas is nearly $4.50 — its highest ever for late September — and diesel prices continue to set records, most recently hitting $6.52.

title: Oil prices see-saw, as markets weigh Trump’s UN speech, potential Saudi pipeline fix
summary: Oil prices erased sharp drops from earlier Tuesday after President Donald Trump said he believes he can reach a deal with Iran to end the war after the midterms.
story: Oil prices see-sawed throughout the day Tuesday as a wave of headlines lifted prices, only to have them move lower again within hours.
Crude’s first big jump of the day came while President Donald Trump was addressing the U.N. General Assembly.
“I believe we will make a deal right after the election because it does not make sense for them not to,” Trump told assembled world leaders.
What markets heard, however, was that there would be no deal before Nov. 3. By the time Trump had finished speaking, prices for both U.S. crude oil and Brent had risen overall for the day.
But they didn’t stay there for long.
During a later meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Trump announced that his team had just concluded a “very good” three-hour meeting with Iran’s representatives.
Trump’s top foreign policy negotiator Steve Witkoff and his son-in-law, Jared Kushner, were the two envoys in the meeting, he said.
The talks appeared to represent genuine progress, sending oil prices down again around 1%.

Global crude prices were also falling in part Tuesday on momentum from reports that Iran had offered to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within days if the U.S. agreed to take steps toward easing pressure on the country.

NBC News has not confirmed this offer, and Fars, Iran’s semi-official news agency, knocked the reports down. “Iranian sources have described these reports as unreliable and untrue,” Fars reported, but did not identify who those sources were.
Trump will be holding a number of meetings with world leaders at the United Nations General Assembly in New York City, including one with Gulf Cooperation Council leaders on Tuesday night.

Along with tumbling oil prices, bond yields also fell Tuesday. The 10-year U.S. Treasury yield, which heavily influences consumer borrowing rates, fell to as low as 4.92% after climbing as high as 5.04% a week ago. That was its highest level since 2007.
The 30-year Treasury yield also dipped to as low as 5.25% Tuesday morning. Last week, it hit 5.4%, a level not seen since 2007.
On Sunday, Trump had signaled a willingness to meet with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio told NBC News on Tuesday that there was nothing “scheduled at this point.”
The U.S., however, would be “open to something like that,” he said.

In the seven months since the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28, vessel traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has ground to a near halt at times.  Traffic did not exceed 20 ships per day over the last week, according to data from MarineTraffic.

Hormuz’s central role in facilitating tanker traffic also helps explain why investors were relieved Tuesday by reports that Saudi Arabia’s key east-west pipeline might be back in operation sooner than expected.
On Sept. 11, the Saudi Energy Ministry said that the pipeline had been shut after “multiple attacks” amid the kingdom’s escalating conflict with the Iran-backed Houthi rebels.
Experts initially feared the closure could last months, cutting off a vital workaround for oil exports while Hormuz remains unstable.

Reuters reported that the pipeline had already restarted and could resume exports from a Red Sea port later in the day, citing three people familiar with the matter. Bloomberg News reported that Saudi Arabia was running tests on the pipeline in the hopes of restarting it this week, citing multiple people familiar with the matter.
The state oil company that operates the pipeline, Saudi Aramco, did not immediately respond to a request for comment from NBC News.

“If you look at the increases we’ve seen in just the last two weeks, the enormous majority of that increase is because the Houthis attacked a Saudi pipeline and the Saudis had to shut down that pipeline,” Rubio said Tuesday on NBC’s “TODAY.”

“So there’s still oil in the system, but the markets are reacting to the expectation that there will not be as much Saudi oil in the future” as a result of the pipeline attack, Rubio added. “That is a problem, as well, that we are confronting here.”

The price per barrel of both oil benchmarks are up more than 60% since the start of the year. So are retail gas prices, which reached $4.47 per gallon on Tuesday. That’s 50% higher than it was when the Iran war began.
The price of diesel has also skyrocketed.

The national average hit a new all-time high of $6.52 per gallon Tuesday, up 82% since the start of the year on a record run propelled in part by intensifying aerial attacks between Russia and Ukraine. Trump is set to hold talks with Zelenskyy on Tuesday as he pushes for an energy truce.

Despite the overall rise in oil and gas prices this month, Trump nonetheless claimed in his UNGA speech that “oil prices will come plummeting down, even lower than they were at the start of the conflict” as soon as the war is over.
Experts doubt that.

At the beginning of the month, multiple Wall Street commodities analysts warned that oil prices could rise to $120 or even $150 per barrel if the Iran war drags on and more energy infrastructure is damaged.

Stocks reacted little to the flood of energy-related headlines Tuesday. The S&P 500 closed flat, while the Nasdaq Composite rose 0.4%. This followed a banner trading day Monday driven by falling oil prices and bond yields.

title: Iowa GOP Senate candidate calls for Iran war to end despite voting to let Trump continue it
summary: Rep. Ashley Hinson, R-Iowa, has voted against House resolutions directing President Donald Trump to halt the war with Iran six times, including as recently as last week.
story: Rep. Ashley Hinson, R-Iowa, has voted against House resolutions directing President Donald Trump to halt the war with Iran six times, including as recently as last week.
But on Monday, the Republican Senate candidate called for an “immediate end” to the conflict.

“Iowans are being squeezed and shouldn’t have to foot the bill at the pump or the checkout line for the war in Iran,” Hinson wrote on X, calling for measures like suspending the gas tax, pausing diesel exports and replenishing the highway trust fund to provide relief from high costs.
“These actions to lower costs are needed ASAP, and the war needs to be brought to a successful and immediate end,” she said.
It drew a quick response from her Democratic opponent, Josh Turek, who also pointed to a seventh vote by Hinson against ending U.S. hostilities in Lebanon as part of the conflict in the Middle East.
In a reply to Hinson, Turek wrote on X, “it’s easy to send a tweet but when you had the chance to vote to end this war, you chose not to.”

“You voted seven times to continue it, including just last week. It’s time to actually end the forever wars and put Iowa and Iowans first,” Turek continued. “Glad you’re finally following my lead after waffling on the proposals I put forward last week to address the rising costs of the war in Iran.”

Last month, the nonpartisan Cook Political Report with Amy Walter shifted its Iowa Senate race rating from “lean Republican” to “toss-up.” Trump won the state in the last three presidential elections, and Democrats haven’t won a Senate race there since 2008.
Hinson’s campaign didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment about her prior votes against the Iran war powers measures in the House.

The latest resolution passed the House 220-204 last Tuesday, with seven Republicans joining all Democrats present in supporting it. Among those seven were Reps. Zach Nunn and Marianette Miller-Meeks of Iowa, who had previously opposed such measures but changed their position.
Both are running for re-election in battleground House districts. The Cook Political Report rates their races as “toss-ups.”

Hinson, a three-term congresswoman, has been increasingly characterizing herself as “bipartisan” and slowly distancing herself from the Trump administration as polls show voters disapprove of the president’s handling of the war and the economy. Her messaging and votes highlight the difficult balance of turning out Trump’s strongest supporters while appealing to the growing number of voters who have soured on him.

Last month, Hinson objected to his proposal to import more foreign beef. Last week, when Vice President JD Vance went to Council Bluffs, Iowa, to rally for Republicans, Hinson did not attend, citing a scheduling conflict.

“I want to make a shoutout to an amazing public servant,” Vance said in his remarks. “I know she couldn’t be here today, but are we going to elect Ashley Hinson the next United States senator from the great state of Iowa?”
Meanwhile, another Midwest Republican Senate candidate running in a tough race on Tuesday said the Iran war must end.
Former Rep. Mike Rogers said in a video released on social media that “the war with Iran needs to end and end quickly.”
“When it does, energy costs will plummet,” Rogers said. “But Michigan families can’t afford to wait for that to happen.”
Similar to Hinson, Rogers said he supported suspending the state and federal gas tax and a temporary embargo on American diesel exports.
In response, Rogers’ Democratic opponent, Abdul El-Sayed said on X, “You’ve spent your entire campaign supporting the war in Iran. Liar, coward, fraud.”

title: Tehran warns of ‘new weapons’ as Trump weighs meeting with Iranian president
summary: Iran warned Monday it would use “new weapons with new capabilities” if the U.S. launched a fresh assault after President Donald Trump ramped up the rhetoric against Tehran over the weekend.
story: Iran warned Monday it would use “new weapons with new capabilities” if the U.S. launched a fresh assault after President Donald Trump ramped up the rhetoric against Tehran over the weekend.

“If a new aggression takes place, we will definitely change the weapons and geography of the war,” Hossein Mohebbi, a spokesman for Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said Monday, according to the semiofficial Fars news agency.
Mohebbi did not provide details on what the new weapons were or which new locations could be hit.

Earlier, Trump said he would “probably” be open to meeting with his Iranian counterpart, President Masoud Pezeshkian, during the United Nations General Assembly this week, Fox News chief foreign correspondent Trey Yingst reported Sunday.

The possibility of a meeting offered a glimmer of hope for a resolution to the nearly seven-month war with Iran, which has resulted in Iran blocking the key Strait of Hormuz, and its Yemeni allies bombing a crucial east-west oil pipeline and threatening another crucial waterway. Resultant economic shock waves have hit the U.S. and the world economy, driving up oil and diesel prices and fueling inflation.

title: U.S. proposes AI alert system with China ahead of Trump-Xi summit
summary: The United States has proposed a new AI safety notification mechanism for President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping to consider at their summit in Washington this week, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Sunday.
story: HONG KONG — The United States has proposed a new AI safety notification mechanism for President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping to consider at their summit in Washington this week, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Sunday, amid global concern over whether the world’s two leading AI powers can work together to contain the technology’s potential dangers.

Speaking to reporters after daylong talks in New York with Chinese officials, Bessent said the two sides had discussed setting up a new U.S.-China AI dialogue that would include a mechanism for alerting each other to AI-related incidents that could affect national security.

“We think that just like with any cross-border activity, that moving from opaque to more transparency between the number one and the number two AI powers in the world is very important,” he said, adding that the two sides had agreed to meet again on the AI issue.
'Godfather of AI': Congress has about a year to get ahead of AI

AI is expected to be high on the agenda when Trump and Xi meet Thursday, especially after warnings from AI leaders in the U.S. that the technology could pose an existential threat within a few years. Trump has dismissed such concerns as a “hoax” while agreeing with AI executives such as Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei that the U.S. must not allow China to pull ahead in the global AI race.

Experts caution that the Trump-Xi summit is unlikely to produce any major agreement on AI, citing the high level of distrust between the two countries. China has interpreted calls to slow down AI development as targeted at its own progress.

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told reporters that AI talks would not affect U.S. export controls on advanced chips and semiconductor manufacturing equipment that have hindered Chinese AI companies.

Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng and China’s chief trade negotiator, Li Chenggang, did not comment to reporters as they left the talks at JPMorganChase headquarters. A Chinese readout of the talks published by Xinhua, China’s state-run news agency, did not mention the U.S. proposal and said only that the two sides had discussed AI.

Xinhua said the two sides also had “frank, in-depth and constructive exchanges on important economic and trade issues of common concern, including implementing the consensus reached in previous trade consultations and promoting bilateral trade and investment.”
A major question ahead of this week’s summit is whether Trump and Xi will agree to extend a fragile trade truce that is set to expire Nov. 10.

Bessent and Greer said the two sides had agreed to operationalize a new “Board of Trade” that was announced during Trump’s visit to Beijing in May, and were exploring the potential for lower tariffs on “non-sensitive” products.

On the Chinese side, Greer said, those could include consumer goods and low-tech items, while U.S. exports of energy, agricultural goods and medical devices are also being considered. He did not say whether that meant tariffs on those items would be lowered now or that they would only be exempted from fresh duties in the future.

“There is a world where you have a relatively small subset of American and Chinese goods that can be traded in a balanced way that are non-sensitive,” he said. “Then in the future, as trade actions come up, we can consider them as a class unto themselves.”
Jennifer Jett reported from Hong Kong, and Steve Kopack and Allie Canal reported from New York.

title: Three dead in Moscow as Ukraine launches massive drone attack while Russia votes
summary: The largest Ukrainian drone attack reported so far on the Moscow region killed two people ⁠and damaged part of an oil refinery in the capital, authorities said Sunday.
story: Ukraine launched hundreds of drones at Moscow on Sunday, killing two people on the final day of a Russian parliamentary election that President Vladimir Putin has cast as a test of support for the war in ⁠Ukraine.

Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Telegram: “In the Moscow region tonight, our long-range responses hit very noticeably. One of the key enterprises of Russia’s oil industry and an aggressor logistics facility were struck.”
He did not specifically mention the ongoing State Duma election, but added that Moscow could “end its brutal war and choose peace” if there is “political will” to do so.
An oil refinery was damaged in the strike, with videos showing smoke billowing out across the city.
In the village of Sofyino, ‌south of Moscow, a body covered in a stained ‌blanket lay in front of a damaged apartment block, the upper windows of which were blown out.
“Glass went flying, people started screaming and shouting. I turned around and the entrance doors had already been blown out, ⁠debris everywhere,” said resident Vitaliy, who gave only his first name.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said over 1,600 drones had been shot down by Russia since Saturday, including 450 heading toward Moscow.
In a Telegram post, he said: “This unprecedented attack was clearly planned with the aim of disrupting the elections. The enemy did not succeed.”

Moscow region governor Andrey Vorobyov said in a Telegram post that a 74-year-old man in the Orekhovo-Zuyevo District and a 44-year-old woman in Ramenskoye were killed in the attack. A third person later died of their injuries.
He said 15 people were hospitalized, including two teenagers, ages 14 and 15.
In a post on X, Ukrainian foreign minister Andrii Sybiha said: “My morning today started with congratulations from many foreign colleagues on Moscow Burning Day.”
He added: “Now that the war has come home, Russians have only Putin to blame for it. The message to him is simple: look out the Kremlin window, see the flames over Moscow — and end this war.”
At the same time, Russia continued its strikes on Ukraine, with three children and a woman killed in strikes in the Kyiv region, regional governor Tymur Tkachenko said in a Telegram post.

Kyiv has demonstrated an increasing ability to strike deep inside Russia in recent months, targeting key military and industrial sites as part of an effort to make everyday Russians feel the cost of the war. Russia has hammered Ukrainian cities across the conflict, now in its fifth year.
The State Duma vote, the first since Russia’s full-scale invasion, is expected to see Putin’s United Russia party easily retain ​its ⁠dominance in a process that critics deride as a farce.
The Kremlin is likely to present the outcome as evidence of public backing for Putin’s policies and for the war.

“Participation in the elections is our joint contribution to Russia’s victory,” Putin declared in a video address to the nation days before the vote. It will serve as a reminder that “millions of people are backing our fighters and that we stand together,” he added.

Election authorities say the ⁠three days of voting have proceeded smoothly despite reported cyberattacks on Saturday. Turnout by late morning on Sunday was at over 45% for the ​Duma vote and ⁠regional elections, said Central Election Commission Chairwoman Ella Pamfilova.
Most anti-war ‌candidates have been barred from the ballot.

Anti-war politician Boris Nadezhdin, who tried to challenge Putin in the presidential election two years ago but was barred from running, told NBC News earlier this week that the elections were “crooked” with no trace of real opposition, though he said disapproval could manifest in a higher number of spoiled ballots or increased tactical voting against Putin’s United Russia party.

Figures from the anti-war Yabloko party said they feared for their freedom after courts handed long jail terms to two senior party figures before the ‌vote. Discrediting the army or spreading what authorities regard as fake ‌news is punishable by lengthy prison sentences.
In a small act of defiance, Yabloko’s leader, Nikolai Rybakov, demonstrably spoiled his ballot paper, writing his party’s name and the slogan “For peace.”

“No one in the world can claim anymore that everyone in Russia supports what is happening,” Rybakov told NBC News last week. “Now everyone has seen that millions of people disagree with what’s going on, and they have turned their attention to Yabloko precisely because it consistently advocates for peace and for an alternative to the status quo.”

Russian electoral officials said Saturday that an online voting system in Moscow had come under cyberattack. Kyiv, which has suspended elections under martial law, has dismissed the Russian vote as a “pseudo election.”

Despite what experts see as the election’s predictable outcome, the NEST think tank in Berlin, co-founded by Kremlin critic Mikhail Khodorkovsky, said the vote could ‌still produce awkward moments for the Kremlin at a time of economic strain.

“The consequences of the war are increasingly being felt within the ​country, and accumulated anxiety and frustration may translate into votes for the systemic opposition parties that the Kremlin has allowed to remain on ‌the ballot,” it said in a note.
Initial results are expected to start emerging at around 2 p.m. ET on Sunday, with more complete results available on Monday.

title: Princess Diana’s brother says King Charles ‘gaslit’ him in dispute over book claims
summary: Princess Diana’s brother, Charles Spencer, has accused King Charles of gaslighting him after Buckingham Palace pushed back at his claims about the monarch’s conduct.
story: Princess Diana’s brother, Charles Spencer, has accused King Charles of gaslighting him after Buckingham Palace pushed back at his claims about the monarch’s conduct.

Buckingham Palace released an unusually forceful statement Wednesday ahead of the release of a memoir by Spencer, which charts the breakdown of then-Prince Charles’ marriage to Princess Diana, and the fallout from her death in a Paris car crash in 1997, one year after the royal couple finalized their divorce.

In an initial excerpt released ahead of publication, Spencer recalled a heated phone call with Charles amid a disagreement about funeral arrangements, claiming that a furious Charles had told him Diana would “soon be forgotten.”

“While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and color memory in ways others do not recognize, even many years after such a loss,” the palace had responded.
In an interview with Britain’s Mail on Sunday newspaper, Spencer said: “It is not every day you wake up to find you’ve been gaslit by the king.”
“It was astonishingly provocative and below the belt because it was essentially trying to say I’d lied without the king being able to deny what I’d said,” Spencer added.
“Gaslighting” is a form of manipulation where the manipulator is trying to get someone to question their own reality, memory or perceptions.
In a further interview with the BBC that aired Sunday, Spencer said he told close friends and family at the time about what Charles had said “because it was so monstrous.”
He also appeared to indicate that Charles and Diana’s sons, heir to the throne Prince William and his brother, Prince Harry, were aware of his allegation before the memoir was published.
“I don’t like to talk about what I’ve been speaking about to William and Harry, but this will not be a surprise to them, I will tell you that. These words will not be a surprise to them,” he said.
There has been no public comment from William or Harry on Spencer’s memoir.

Spencer, an earl whose aristocratic family has generational ties with Britain’s royal family, denied that the book, published after years of silence, was motivated by money or score-settling. “I have a duty, as an eyewitness to history, in the final season of my life,” he told the BBC. “I wanted to just put things down that were true.”

He added: “This is not a threat, it’s a fact: I know lots of things about the king which I chose not to include in the book, because they were not relevant. I’m a historian. ... I wanted to give the context.”
Spencer’s book, “Swan Song: Diana, My Sister,” is due to be released publicly on Tuesday.

In other excerpts from the book, published in advance by the Daily Mail newspaper, Spencer writes that Charles sounded “giddily elated” and “like a lottery winner” when they spoke by phone immediately after Diana’s death, adding: “I suspect the prince’s first reaction must have been to think more of how this event might free him to marry the woman he loved, rather than appreciating the loss of one he did not.”
He also speaks about his sister’s mental health and recounts conversations with her, saying she had told him how “things became very difficult indeed in the marriage early on.”

The book also includes an allegation that Diana suspected Charles was “in love with” a member of royal staff during their marriage, separate from his relationship with the now-Queen Camilla, though Spencer says he has no evidence that was true.
Since its initial statement, Buckingham Palace has remained silent on the further allegations in Spencer’s book. The palace again declined to comment Sunday.

Prince Harry, who quit as a working royal six years ago amid a reported rift with senior royals, has remained close to the Spencer family, with his own memoir “Spare” thanking “my mother’s siblings for their love, support, time, and perspective.”

Of his relationship with Harry, Spencer said: “There’s this perception in the media that I’m on Harry’s side. Well, I’m on my deceased sister’s sons’ side, both of them, and if either of them wanted anything, then I’d be equally there for them. I never get involved in one camp or the other, except as a benign figure, I hope.”
The royal family continued to undertake public duties this week even as Spencer’s book has dominated the headlines, with Charles also meeting with senior figures in AI at a summit in Scotland.

title: Diana’s brother says Charles sounded ‘giddily elated’ after her death
summary: Buckingham Palace remains gripped in drama as excerpts of Princess Diana’s brother’s book continues to be dripped into the public domain, ahead of its official release next week.
story: LONDON — King Charles III is facing more criticism from Princess Diana’s brother, Charles Spencer, with Buckingham Palace bracing for days of revelations from his tell-all memoir.

The latest advance excerpt from the book accuses the then-Prince Charles of sounding “giddily elated” and “like a lottery winner,” immediately after Diana’s death in a Paris car crash in 1997, one year after they finalized their divorce.

Spencer, an earl whose aristocratic family has generational ties with Britain’s royal family, writes that he was at his home in South Africa with his children when he learned “in the middle of the night” from his sister Jane Fellowes that Diana had been in a car crash. He later learned, “after escalating dread,” that she had died.

“The phone rang constantly. Prince Charles caught me as I crossed the landing upstairs,” he wrote. “Unlike my other callers, who were stunned, barely able to articulate their condolences and offers of help, he sounded giddily elated — like a lottery winner, I remember thinking at the time.”
On the call, Spencer wrote, Charles told him that he had informed Princes William and Harry, then 15 and 12, of their mother’s death.

“Looking back now, I suspect the prince’s first reaction must have been to think more of how this event might free him to marry the woman he loved, rather than appreciating the loss of one he did not. It can be hard to feel too much sympathy for an ex-spouse, or those who care for them profoundly, after bitter divorce,” he added.

Spencer also detailed feeling shut out by royal protocol during Diana’s funeral arrangements, alleging that royal officials turned down a request to play music loved by Diana — Mozart’s “Requiem” —  during her funeral.
“Diana remained theirs, in Buckingham Palace’s eyes, even in death. Her family, despite her divorce, were simply expected to fall into line with any royal decisions,” he added.
In the first wave of revelations from the book earlier this week, Spencer alleged that Charles had told him that Diana would soon be forgotten in the days after her death.
Buckingham Palace released an unusually forceful statement denying Spencer’s claims and suggesting that grief for his older sister may have impacted his memory.

“While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and color memory in ways others do not recognize, even many years after such a loss,” the statement said Wednesday.
A spokeswoman for Buckingham Palace declined to further comment Friday, telling NBC News that “we do not comment on books as a policy,” and referring to Wednesday’s statement.
Speaking to the BBC Friday, Spencer pushed back at the palace’s statement, maintaining: “I can tell you here and now, those are exactly the words he said.”
Noting the wording of the palace statement, he added: “I don’t hear him saying he didn’t say that.”

Spencer’s book, “Swan Song: Diana, My Sister,” is due to be released publicly Tuesday. Britain’s Daily Mail newspaper is publishing excerpts in advance, while an interview with Spencer is due to air on CBS on Sunday.
Thursday’s tranche of new excerpts continued to provide difficult reading for the palace, reflecting on the breakdown of Diana and Charles’ marriage.
Spencer writes that his sister “told me that things became very difficult indeed in the marriage early on, and I am sure that both spouses despaired of the other at times.”
“I am not hypocritical enough to judge or criticise anyone else’s marital record. I am merely recording how my sister felt and am not assessing whether she was right or not,” he added.

Spencer also writes about Diana’s struggle with an eating disorder, which she spoke about during her lifetime, as well as her wider mental state, criticizing her transfer from a long-serving family doctor to a royal physician.

“It is a sad fact that, in her later years, Diana drove herself more than once to Beachy Head, the highest chalk sea cliff in England, while contemplating ending it all. Her love for her sons stopped her from going further,” he writes.

The royal family continued to undertake a busy schedule of public duties this week. Charles made headlines at an event meeting with senior figures in AI at a summit in Scotland, while the Prince and Princess of Wales, William and Kate, attended charitable events there.

Prince Harry, who returned to the United Kingdom last month but remains a nonworking member of the royal family, was also photographed for the first time since his return, at a charitable function Thursday.

Harry, whose own bombshell memoir “Spare” rattled the royal establishment in 2023, has remained close to the Spencer family, with his own book thanking “my mother’s siblings for their love, support, time, and perspective.”
He did not respond to questions shouted by reporters about his uncle’s book Thursday.

title: Trump administration grants visas to top Iranian leaders to attend U.N. General Assembly
summary: The decision to grant Iranian leaders visas to travel to New York City for the annual meeting of global leaders comes seven months into the U.S. war with Iran.
story: The Trump administration will allow an Iranian delegation to attend the United Nations General Assembly next week, albeit with some restrictions, a State Department spokesperson said Thursday.
The decision to grant Iranian top officials visas to travel to New York City for the annual meeting of global leaders comes seven months into the U.S. war with Iran.

“Consistent with our host country obligations, the core delegation from the Iranian regime will be able to attend U.N. General Assembly High Level Week,” the spokesperson said in a statement. “The delegation will be under travel restrictions and will face prohibitions on the purchase of luxury and other goods per our policy.”

The Iranian delegation’s trip comes at a sensitive time, as the U.S. military and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps have continued attacks in the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway through which some 20% of the world’s oil flowed before the war.
President Donald Trump said Thursday that he is considering resuming full-scale attacks against Iran.
“I have a big decision coming up. Do I want to go in and annihilate them [the Iranian regime] or do I not? It’s a big decision. Anything could happen with me,” Trump told Axios.
Last week, the U.S. military struck five Iranian tankers linked to the IRGC in response to attempted attacks on an American warship, according to U.S. Central Command.

The Iranian delegation cleared by the U.S. will be smaller than the one the country sent last year, the State Department said. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi will be a part of the delegation receiving U.S. visas, a U.S. source familiar with the decision said.

The U.S. has historically restricted the Iranian delegation’s travel during its visits to New York, but beginning in 2025 the Trump administration began blocking the officials’ access even to wholesale and luxury stores, confining their movements to “areas strictly necessary to transit to and from the U.N. headquarters district to conduct their official U.N. business,” according to the State Department.

“We will not let the Iranian regime’s elites exploit UNGA for a luxury retail splurge paid for by the Iranian people’s suffering, all while the regime funnels Iran’s wealth to support its terrorist proxies,” State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott said Thursday on social media. “The U.S. will continue to ban Iranian UN Mission officials, visiting officials, and their dependents from buying wholesale club memberships or luxury goods here.”

Last month, an Iranian presidential protocol official said Tehran was still assessing the level and size of its attendance at the General Assembly this year, calling the conditions imposed by the U.S. illegal, without elaborating on the complaint.

The general debate of the General Assembly, the part of the meeting where world leaders will give speeches, will begin on Tuesday when Trump is expected to speak. Pezeshkian is scheduled to address the General Assembly on Wednesday.

Despite granting visas to the Iranian delegation, the Trump administration will once again block Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas from attending the General Assembly, according to a source familiar with the decision.

That decision is an extension of sanctions that deny the necessary visas to officials from the Palestinian Authority and the Palestine Liberation Organization to attend the annual meeting of global leaders, according to the source.

In a statement Wednesday, the State Department accused both organizations of trying to bypass negotiations by seeking unilateral recognition of a Palestinian state, taking actions to internationalize the Israeli-Palestinian conflict — including through the International Criminal Court and the International Court of Justice — and “glorifying acts of terrorism and terrorists in public pronouncements and school textbooks.”

The Palestinian Authority’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Expatriates rejected the U.S. decision and said in a statement that “the unjustified measure” runs counter to efforts aimed at restoring trust and “creating the political climate necessary to implement the two-state solution and achieve peace and stability in the region.”

title: King Charles issues fiery response to Princess Diana’s brother over claims in new book
summary: In a rare rebuke, Buckingham Palace issued a robust statement aimed at King Charles III’s former brother-in-law, Earl Charles Spencer, as he is set to release his bombshell memoir.
story: LONDON — Buckingham Palace has issued a rare and unusually forceful denial after the late Princess Diana’s brother claimed that the then-Prince Charles said his first wife would soon be forgotten in the days after her death.
In a soon-to-be-published memoir, Charles Spencer recounts the emotional days in the aftermath of Diana’s 1997 death in a Paris car crash at age 36.

An excerpt published Wednesday alleges a heated exchange with Charles, now the British king, over whether Princes William and Harry — then 15 and 12 — should walk behind their mother’s coffin in the funeral procession.

Spencer says he expressed that Diana would not want them to endure such an ordeal and claims that was met with a “stream of anger” from Charles. He writes that Charles “unleashed down the phone what I have always taken to be his pent-up contempt for Diana, and his horror that the world was so bowled over by her death. ‘Rest assured,’ he hissed, ‘we’ll forget her soon enough.’”
Buckingham Palace replied with a forceful statement denying the claims and suggesting that grief for his older sister may have affected Spencer’s memory.

“While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and color memory in ways others do not recognize, even many years after such a loss,” said the statement, released Wednesday.
Diana’s 1997 funeral procession is etched into modern memory.
Her brother and two young sons were among those who walked solemnly behind her coffin as it passed through central London.

India McTaggart, a royal correspondent at The Telegraph newspaper, told NBC News about Wednesday’s statement: “Earl Spencer’s book is expected to contain a number of incendiary claims, and perhaps this was the palace trying to get on the front foot and get ahead of some of the allegations we expect to see.”
The royal family mostly avoided commenting in 2023, when Prince Harry published his autobiography, “Spare,” which also generated global headlines with claims of bitter family feuds.

Queen Elizabeth II famously issued a brief but forceful statement in 2021 after Harry and his wife, Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, alleged racism in the family. “Recollections may vary,” the late queen said.
McTaggart said that “the palace will certainly be bracing for more headlines” as a result of the new memoir.

“At the same time, we’ll see Harry carrying out public engagements this week, while the king and the prince and princess of Wales continue with theirs. It will be interesting to see how all of that is covered now that they’re all in Britain at the same time.”

Diana was one of the most photographed women in the world after she married Charles in 1981. Their high-profile marriage ended in 1996, and she died a year later after being chased by paparazzi with her partner, Dodi Fayed. Her death in a Paris tunnel brought the world to a standstill.

At the time of her funeral, the royal family received criticism from the public and the media for appearing to be slow to react to the outpouring of love and grief from the public for a woman posthumously dubbed the “people’s princess.”
Spencer’s book, “Swan Song: Diana, My Sister,” is due to be published Tuesday. Britain’s Daily Mail newspaper is publishing excerpts in advance.

title: Australian athlete apologizes after winning race despite involuntary bowel movement
summary: “Looking back, I regret the decision to not have stepped off the track,” Hyrox competitor Joanna Wietrzyk said.
story: An Australian athlete apologized Thursday for continuing — and winning — her race in China over the weekend after experiencing an involuntary bowel movement during competition.
Joanna Wietrzyk, a 24-year-old from Melbourne, said she should have pulled off the track during the women’s 16-to-24 Hyrox event in Beijing on Saturday.
The athlete said she hadn’t felt any symptoms before the race that might have warned her about what was to come.
“I want to offer my sincere apology to the people of China, my fellow competitors, the spectators and the HYROX organizers for what happened during the race in Beijing,” Wietrzyk said in a statement.

“I felt completely fit and healthy at the start of the race, with no reason to expect any illness. Looking back, I regret the decision to not have stepped off the track. I recognize that I should have made a different choice. I take responsibility for my decision to continue and am deeply sorry for the discomfort and disruption it caused.”

Hyrox is a relatively new indoor sport that combines running and performing high-intensity exercises at various workout stations. It’s not an Olympic sport, but its backers hope it could make the Games in 2032 or 2036.

“I know my actions had an impact beyond myself, and I am genuinely sorry to everyone who was affected,” Wietrzyk said. “I am learning from this experience and will carry those lessons with me, including remembering that there is more to life than racing and knowing when it is right to step away.”
Hyrox co-founder Moritz Fürste apologized for the incident on Sunday and said organizers should have intervened immediately.
Wietrzyk’s time of 1:01:23 would have put her atop her division, but she has asked to “retroactively withdraw” from competition.

“On reflection, I have decided to retroactively withdraw from the race and forfeit the points I earned,” Wietrzyk said. “Thank you to those standing by me, both as an athlete and as a person, during this time, and to everyone who has reached out with kindness and support. It means more to me than I can properly express right now. I will be taking some time to recover, reflect and look after myself and my family away from the noise.”

title: How Canada and the E.U. are teaming up to counter Trump
summary: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney addressed the European Parliament in Strasbourg to lay out how middle powers might counteract Trump’s hostility.
story: Around 3,700 miles separate the Gothic towers of Canada’s Parliament in Ottawa from the glass-fronted modern European Parliament building in eastern France.
But judging by the thunderous applause shaking the E.U. chamber Thursday, President Donald Trump’s threats are helping to close that distance.

Canada and Europe have long been close U.S. allies, benefiting from American military power and trading heft. But Trump has upended those relationships, waging trade wars against Canada and the E.U., while threatening to absorb Canada as America’s 51st state and take control of Greenland, Denmark’s autonomous Arctic territory.
Without a reliable partner in the White House, the spurned allies are now forging their own path.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney urged the world’s “middle powers” to join forces in a speech before the European Parliament in Strasbourg on Thursday to create “an alliance strong enough so that no one can dictate our choices.”
The strategy in short: strength in numbers.
“I’m not proposing a third bloc in order to become a great power rival, only with better manners,” he stressed.

“We do not seek power to dominate others,” Carney continued. “On the contrary, we are pursuing resilience. So no one — no one — can control our open markets, impair our sovereignty, threaten our territorial integrity or undermine our freedoms, our democracies, our rule of law.”

The remarks appeared aimed in part at Trump, though Carney did not name the president in his speech. The response in the room was a near-unanimous standing ovation from lawmakers representing the bloc’s 27 member countries.
Some European leaders, meanwhile, appear ready to grant Canada more favorable access to its closely guarded single market.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen caused a stir Wednesday when she suggested making Canada the E.U.’s first “associate member.” She also outlined an “alliance for the future” that would increase cooperation on defense, energy, critical minerals, artificial intelligence and other tech.
“This is a partnership not against anyone else, but for our common strength,” she said.

At a news conference Thursday, Carney stressed that Canada was “not in a position, nor seeking, to become a full member” of the European Union, a long and drawn-out process of regulatory alignment that can sometimes take decades for applicant countries.
“What matters is the substance,” he said of the associate membership proposal.

Carney has deep links to Europe, having served as governor of the Bank of England before his political homecoming propelled him to Canada’s leadership. He tapped into those ties Wednesday, bonding with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham at an Everton soccer match.

title: New wild cat species is identified for first time in 100 years, researchers say
summary: Researchers say they’ve identified a new species of wild cat previously unknown to science. The Tilcayo tiger cat is smaller than a typical house cat and lives in the Bolivian cloud forest.
story: For the first time in a century, researchers say they’ve identified a new species of wild cat previously unknown to science.

Leopardus tilcayo — or the tilcayo tiger cat — is slender and spotted, with rounded ears. It is smaller than a typical house cat and lives in the Bolivian Yungas, the cloud forest where the Andes mountains meet the Amazon basin. The species was described for the first time in the journal Current Biology on Thursday.
Researchers identify new species of wild cat

It’s rare to find a new, relatively large mammal. Unsurprisingly, most newly discovered animal species are small in size, said Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz, who co-authored the study and leads a wild cat conservation program called Programa de Investigación de Félidos Bolivia (Bolivian Felid Research and Conservation Program).
“This time, it’s a cat. That’s really novel. And it hasn’t happened in 100 years,” she said. “No one else had named it. No one else had described it.”
The size of the Leopardus tilcayo population is not clear yet.

“We really don’t know how many cats are still in the wild,” said Nogales-Ascarrunz, whose work as a conservationist is funded by National Geographic. “We need science, we need more studies to answer this question, which is actually critical for its conservation.”
